SECTION I
L	Today, many people see democracy as under threat in a way that only a decade ago seemed
unimaginable. Following the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, it seemed like democracy was the way
of the future. But nowadays, the state of democracy looks very different; we hear about
‘backsliding’ and ‘decay’ and other descriptions of a sort of creeping authoritarianism. Some long-
established democracies, such as the United States, are witnessing a violation of governmental
norms once thought secure, and this has culminated in the recent insurrection at the US Capitol.
If democracy is a torch that shines for a time before burning out — think of Classical Athens and
Renaissance city republics — it all feels as if we might be heading toward a new period of darkness.
What can we do to reverse this apparent trend and support democracy?
First, we must dispense with the idea that democracy is like a torch that gets passed from one
leading society to another. The core feature of democracy — that those who rule can do so only with
the consent of the people — wasn’t invented in one place at one time: it evolved independently in a
great many human societies.
Over several millennia and across multiple continents, early democracy was an institution in
which rulers governed jointly with councils and assemblies of the people. From the Huron (who
called themselves the Wendats) and the Iroquois (who called themselves the Haudenosaunee) in
the Northeastern Woodlands of North America, to the republics of Ancient India, to examples of
city governance in ancient Mesopotamia, these councils and assemblies were common. Classical
Greece provided particularly important instances of this democratic practice, and it’s true that the
Greeks gave us a language for thinking about democracy, including the word demokratia itself.
But they didn’t invent the practice. If we want to better understand the strengths and weaknesses
of our modern democracies, then early democratic societies from around the world provide
important lessons. The core feature of early democracy was that the people had power, even if
multiparty elections (today, often thought to be a definitive feature of democracy) didn’t happen.
The people, or at least some significant fraction of them, exercised this power in many different
ways. In some cases, a ruler was chosen by a council or assembly, and was limited to being first
among equals.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://aeon.co/essays/democracy-is-common-
and-robust-historically-and-across-the-globe

L	Today, many people see democracy as under threat in a way that only a decade ago seemed
unimaginable. Following the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, it seemed like democracy was the way
of the future. But nowadays, the state of democracy looks very different; we hear about
‘backsliding’ and ‘decay’ and other descriptions of a sort of creeping authoritarianism. Some long-
established democracies, such as the United States, are witnessing a violation of governmental
norms once thought secure, and this has culminated in the recent insurrection at the US Capitol.
If democracy is a torch that shines for a time before burning out — think of Classical Athens and
Renaissance city republics — it all feels as if we might be heading toward a new period of darkness.
What can we do to reverse this apparent trend and support democracy?
First, we must dispense with the idea that democracy is like a torch that gets passed from one
leading society to another. The core feature of democracy — that those who rule can do so only with
the consent of the people — wasn’t invented in one place at one time: it evolved independently in a
great many human societies.
Over several millennia and across multiple continents, early democracy was an institution in
which rulers governed jointly with councils and assemblies of the people. From the Huron (who
called themselves the Wendats) and the Iroquois (who called themselves the Haudenosaunee) in
the Northeastern Woodlands of North America, to the republics of Ancient India, to examples of
city governance in ancient Mesopotamia, these councils and assemblies were common. Classical
Greece provided particularly important instances of this democratic practice, and it’s true that the
Greeks gave us a language for thinking about democracy, including the word demokratia itself.
But they didn’t invent the practice. If we want to better understand the strengths and weaknesses
of our modern democracies, then early democratic societies from around the world provide
important lessons. The core feature of early democracy was that the people had power, even if
multiparty elections (today, often thought to be a definitive feature of democracy) didn’t happen.
The people, or at least some significant fraction of them, exercised this power in many different
ways. In some cases, a ruler was chosen by a council or assembly, and was limited to being first
among equals.

II.	We all know people with very different levels of motivation. Some will go the extra mile in any
endeavour. Others just can’t be bothered to put the effort in. We might think of them as lazy —
happiest on the sofa, rather than planning their latest project. What’s behind this variation? Most
of us would probably attribute it to a mixture of temperament, circumstances, upbringing or even
values.
But research in neuroscience and in patients with brain disorders is challenging these
assumptions by revealing the brain mechanisms that underlie motivation. When these systems
become dysfunctional, people who were once highly motivated can become pathologically
apathetic. Whereas previously they might have been curious, highly engaged and productive — at
work, in their social lives and in their creative thinking — they can suddenly seem like the
opposite. For example, in my clinic, I saw a young man called David who had been a high-flyer in
his firm but suddenly lost interest in his job as well as the people around him. Previously, he’d
been a productive and outgoing person who always seemed to take the initiative at work and in his
social circle, but now David did very little and didn’t seem to care. As he put it, he felt he lacked
the motivation to act. Eventually, he was fired from his job but reacted with complete indifference.
He couldn’t even be bothered to register for unemployment benefits. Seeing that he was unable to
pay his rent, David’s friends offered him a room in their house. They soon regretted it. He did
nothing all day, waiting for his mates to come home to cook for him. His GP tried him on an
antidepressant, but it had no effect.
David wasn’t depressed, though. In fact, he was quite happy. After looking deeper into his case, we
discovered that the cause was actually two tiny strokes, one on each side of the brain. These were
located in the basal ganglia, nuclei that are crucial for motivated behaviour. Research in animals

and humans has shown that the basal ganglia connect our needs and wants to actions. When the
basal ganglia are dysfunctional, people don’t initiate actions even though they are able to do so if
they are prompted. David, for example, could put the rubbish out or clean the house if he was
asked. But left to his own devices he did nothing. Studies in people who develop apathy have
shown that many of them just don’t find it sufficiently rewarding to take action. The cost of
making the effort doesn’t seem worth the potential benefit.

Til.	In the Old Library at Trinity College Dublin, a 433-year-old university in Ireland’s capital, rows of
alcoves with dark oak bookcases line the central Long Room, whose Corinthian pillars stretch past
the upper galleries to meet the carved timber ribs of the arched wooden ceiling. When I visited the
library in late spring, the muted morning light from a tall window illuminated the books in one of
the bays. A slender wooden ladder was suspended from a rail above the shelves, ready to reach the
highest levels, where the spines of old leather books were lined up, their gold-tooled letters
catching the light. Standing there, I felt as if this scene had remained undisturbed for hundreds of
years. In reality, however, major changes are on the horizon for this beloved cultural institution—
Ireland’s largest library.
The Old Library is currently undergoing an ambitious redevelopment project that will combine
medieval traditions with new technology and move hundreds of thousands of books at a cost of
more than $100 million. In addition to protecting the early 18th-century building, the project will
ensure the preservation of precious old texts and manuscripts, plus the valuable knowledge they
contain, for future generations. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Trinity staff escalated their efforts to properly safeguard the library and its priceless collections in
the aftermath of a 2019 fire that devastated Paris’ Notre-Dame Cathedral. The Old Library
Redevelopment Project kicked off in 2022 and will begin its restoration and construction phase in
2027, with work estimated to be completed in 2030, according to the library’s chief manuscript
conservator, John Gillis. The project will address pollution and dust accumulation on the books
and introduce building improvements like air purification, environmental controls and fire
protection. So, while the shelves in the Old Library are normally full (stacked side by side, the
books would stretch more than 6.5 miles), on the day I visited, most of them stood empty. Nearly
200,000 books have been moved out thus far, leaving just eight bays where tomes have been left in
place to give visitors—up to one million annually—an idea of what the shelves look like when full.
The curved ribs of the Long Room’s ceiling almost form the inverse of the raised stitching on the
spines of the old books.

content.passageText:
Til.	In the Old Library at Trinity College Dublin, a 433-year-old university in Ireland’s capital, rows of
alcoves with dark oak bookcases line the central Long Room, whose Corinthian pillars stretch past
the upper galleries to meet the carved timber ribs of the arched wooden ceiling. When I visited the
library in late spring, the muted morning light from a tall window illuminated the books in one of
the bays. A slender wooden ladder was suspended from a rail above the shelves, ready to reach the
highest levels, where the spines of old leather books were lined up, their gold-tooled letters
catching the light. Standing there, I felt as if this scene had remained undisturbed for hundreds of
years. In reality, however, major changes are on the horizon for this beloved cultural institution—
Ireland’s largest library.
The Old Library is currently undergoing an ambitious redevelopment project that will combine
medieval traditions with new technology and move hundreds of thousands of books at a cost of
more than $100 million. In addition to protecting the early 18th-century building, the project will
ensure the preservation of precious old texts and manuscripts, plus the valuable knowledge they
contain, for future generations. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Trinity staff escalated their efforts to properly safeguard the library and its priceless collections in
the aftermath of a 2019 fire that devastated Paris’ Notre-Dame Cathedral. The Old Library
Redevelopment Project kicked off in 2022 and will begin its restoration and construction phase in
2027, with work estimated to be completed in 2030, according to the library’s chief manuscript
conservator, John Gillis. The project will address pollution and dust accumulation on the books
and introduce building improvements like air purification, environmental controls and fire
protection. So, while the shelves in the Old Library are normally full (stacked side by side, the
books would stretch more than 6.5 miles), on the day I visited, most of them stood empty. Nearly
200,000 books have been moved out thus far, leaving just eight bays where tomes have been left in
place to give visitors—up to one million annually—an idea of what the shelves look like when full.
The curved ribs of the Long Room’s ceiling almost form the inverse of the raised stitching on the
spines of the old books.

content.passageText:
IV.	Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher, thought that if we are distressed about
something external, “the pain is not due to the thing itself, but to your estimate of it; and this you
have the power to revoke at any moment.”
I love this, but also know from experience that finding that power can be near impossible at times.
We can’t just click our fingers and be rid of, say, grief, or the stress of work, or health worries.
When we are lost in the forest, our fear might not be directly caused by the forest, or our being lost
in said forest, but while we are actively lost in the forest it very much feels like the source of our
fear is being lost in the forest.
But it is helpful to remember that our perspective is our world. And our external circumstances
don’t need to change in order for our perspective to change. And the forests we find ourselves in
are metaphorical, and sometimes we are unable to escape them, but with a change of perspective
we can live among the trees.
Source: Power - The Comfort Book

VII. Air pollution across Delhi-NCR pushed into another dangerous stretch this week, with several
stations logging AQI readings above 600. The spike also left many neighbouring regions, including
Noida, Greater Noida, Ghaziabad, Gurugram and Faridabad, inside the severe bracket and raised
immediate concerns about exposure and health risks for residents. Governments in Delhi-NCR
must act in accordance with the GRAP mechanism as air pollution levels rise through various
stages. There are four stages in GRAP, each linked to the Air Quality Index (AQI) at the time.
When the AQI is 201-300 or the air quality is categorised as ‘poor’, GRAP-I or the first stage of the
framework kicks in. Stage I focuses on early curbs. Stopping open waste burning, removing coal
use in small eateries, and deploying local checks on dust and emissions. The second stage is
invoked when the air quality becomes ‘very poor’ or the AQI is 301-400. Stage II brings in stronger
steps: a halt on diesel generator sets except for essential services, higher parking fees, dust-control
sprinkling, and tighter movement for BS-IV diesel vehicles. GRAP-III is arrived at when the
pollution is ‘severe’ or AQI is 401-450. Stage III restrictions continue across NCR. This includes: A
ban on non-essential construction - piling, excavation, demolition, prohibition on BS-III and BS-IV
diesel vehicles across Delhi-NCR, monitoring of mines, stone crushers and diesel-run machinery
and possible closure of lower classes in schools. Penalties for repeated violations. During GRAP-
IV, conditions enter the ‘severet+’ range. A host of measures are being taken by the Delhi-NCR
administrations under GRAP-IV.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://www.downtoearth.org.in/air/what-is-
grap-iv-now-in-force-in-delhi-and-the-national-capital-region

IX.	The President of India has given assent to the Viksit Bharat—Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika
Mission (Gramin) (VB—G RAM G) Bill, 2025 marking a significant milestone in the
transformation of rural employment policy. Anchored in the principles of empowerment, growth,
convergence and saturation, the Act seeks to transform rural employment from a standalone
welfare intervention into an integrated instrument of development. It strengthens income security
for rural households, modernises governance and accountability, and links wage employment with
the creation of durable and productive rural assets, thereby laying the foundation for a prosperous
and resilient Bharat. All works are planned through a bottom-up process, and all assets created
are aggregated into the Viksit Bharat National Rural Infrastructure Stack, ensuring convergence
of public investments, avoidance of fragmentation, and outcome-based planning aimed at
saturation of critical rural infrastructure, based on varying local needs. The Act reinforces the

right to demand employment while deepening decentralised, participatory governance. It
integrates transparent, rule-based funding, accountability mechanisms, technology-enabled
inclusion and convergence-driven development to ensure that rural employment not only provides
income security but also contributes to sustainable livelihoods, resilient assets and long-term rural
prosperity. The Act removes earlier dis-entitlement provisions and restores unemployment
allowance as a meaningful statutory safeguard. Where employment is not provided within the
stipulated period. The Act is implemented as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, to be notified and
operationalised by the State Governments in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Funding is
provided through State-wise normative allocations based on objective parameters, ensuring
predictability, fiscal discipline, and sound planning, while fully preserving statutory entitlements
to employment.

SECTION III
X.	The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 is a foundational statute governing the transfer of property
between living persons in India. Its general principles provide clarity, fairness and legal certainty
in property transactions by defining the rights, obligations and limitations of parties involved.
These principles ensure orderly transfer of property, restrict arbitrary alienation, and prevent
disputes arising from uncertainty, fraud or overlapping claims. By regulating how and when
property can be transferred, the Act safeguards ownership rights and promotes transparency in
dealings.
The Act plays a vital role in economic development by enabling smooth and secure property
transactions, which are essential for investment and growth in the real estate sector. Principles
such as the rule against perpetuity, doctrine of lis pendens and fraudulent transfer protect long-
term public interest while balancing private rights. Together, these rules create predictability in
property law and contribute to stability in the property market.
The general principles of the Transfer of Property Act include transferability of property under
Section 6, which establishes that property of any kind may be transferred unless expressly
prohibited by law. Section 10 restricts absolute restraints on alienation, ensuring free circulation
of property while permitting limited restraints in specific cases. Section 13 regulates transfer to an
unborn person by requiring creation of a prior interest, while Section 14 embodies the rule against
perpetuity to prevent indefinite control over property.
Sections 19 and 21 distinguish vested and contingent interests to determine when rights accrue.
Section 25 recognises conditional transfers dependent on fulfilment of specified conditions. Section
48 lays down the doctrine of priority, giving precedence to earlier transfers. Section 41 validates
transfers by ostensible owners when the transferee acts in good faith after reasonable inquiry.
Section 43 applies estoppel, preventing transferors from denying authority once they have induced
reliance.
Section 52 incorporates the doctrine of lis pendens, making transfers during litigation subject to
the outcome of the suit. Section 53 renders fraudulent transfers voidable to protect creditors, while
Section 53A embodies the doctrine of part performance, protecting transferees who have acted on
an agreement despite lack of registration. Collectively, these principles form the backbone of
Indian property law, ensuring lawful, fair and effective transfer of property.

focus/loans/home-loan/transfer-of-property-act-india.html

Nisha is protected because part performance, protects a transferee who has acted on an

Nisha is not protected because any unregistered agreement is void and cannot be relied upon

will by the owner who has given the possession.

XI.	Under Sections 11 and 12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, persons competent to contract are
those who have attained the age of majority, are of sound mind, and are not disqualified by law. A
person attains majority at 18 years, or 21 years where a court-appointed guardian exists.
Soundness of mind requires the capacity to understand the contract and form a rational judgment
regarding its effect at the time of contracting. Any person disqualified by law, such as minors,
convicts, insolvents, alien enemies, or foreign sovereigns, is incompetent to contract.
A minor, as defined under the Indian Majority Act, 1875, is incapable of contracting. The nature of
a minor’s agreement was conclusively settled in Mohiri Bibi v. Dharmodas Ghosh, where the Privy
Council held that a minor’s agreement is void ab initio. Such an agreement creates no rights or
obligations, Sections 64 and 65 do not apply, and estoppel cannot operate against a minor even if
minority was falsely represented. A minor is generally not liable in contract or in tort arising
directly out of contract, though liability may arise for independent torts.
The doctrine of restitution, now embodied in Section 33 of the Specific Relief Act, empowers courts
to order restoration of benefits received by a minor, either when the minor seeks cancellation of an
instrument or successfully resists enforcement. However, such relief is discretionary and limited to
the extent of benefit actually received. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Certain contracts beneficial to minors are recognised. A minor may enforce a contract of marriage,
though it cannot be enforced against the minor. Apprenticeship contracts are binding under
statute, but contracts of service are not. A minor cannot be a partner, nor can they ratify a void
contract upon attaining majority, unless fresh consideration is provided.
Under Section 68, a minor’s estate is liable for necessaries supplied to them or their dependants,
provided such goods are suitable to their station in life and not already sufficiently supplied. This
liability is quasi-contractual and rests on the minor’s estate, not personal liability.
Persons of unsound mind are governed by Section 12. Capacity depends on mental condition at the
time of contracting. Temporary insanity, drunkenness, or delirium negates capacity, while lucid
intervals permit valid contracts. Finally, persons disqualified by law include alien enemies during
wartime, convicts during sentence, insolvents regarding property, and foreign sovereigns who
enjoy contractual immunity unless jurisdiction is submitted.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://origiin.com /competency-of-parties-to-a-
contract-under-indian-contract-act-1872/

XII. Capacity in tort law refers to the legal status of a person to sue or to be sued for violation of law.
Although, as a general rule, all persons may sue or be sued in tort, this is not absolute and is
subject to reasonable restrictions. Indian law largely follows English tort principles on disabilities
of parties. Parties to torts include plaintiffs (who initiate proceedings) and defendants (who
defend), and only those having the right to control proceedings or appeal are true parties; others
are privies. Proper joinder of parties is vital, as suing the wrong party or misjoinder/non-joinder
may weaken the plaintiffs case.
Certain persons face limitations in being sued or suing. Traditionally, married women could not
sue or be sued alone due to the common-law unity of spouses, but this disability was removed by
reforms like the Married Women’s Property Act, enabling independent suits. Minors can be sued
for torts like assault, defamation, fraud, etc., but may be exempt where intention or knowledge is
essential, as in Walmsey v. Humonick. Governments and municipalities may avoid liability for
acts done in discharge of sovereign functions, though liability may arise when the act is connected
with assigned duties, as in U.O.I. v. Sugrabai. A lunatic cannot be sued for acts done while not ina
stable state of mind. Alien enemies cannot be sued or sue without Central Government
permission. Corporations, having separate legal personality, can sue and be sued; however,
liability depends on whether the servant acted within authority, as illustrated in Poulton v.
London and S.W. Rly. Co. Foreign sovereigns and ambassadors enjoy immunity unless consent
and jurisdictional submission exist.
Joint tortfeasors are persons who aid, counsel, direct, or join in committing a wrongful act,
creating joint or joint-and-several responsibility. Contribution allows a tortfeasor who pays more
than his share to recover from others. Indian courts have approached English common law
cautiously; in Khushro S. Gandhi v. Guzdar, the Supreme Court held that release of all joint
tortfeasors requires full satisfaction. Joint liability commonly arises through agency, vicarious
liability, and joint action. Ex turpi causa non oritur actio bars claims arising from unlawful
conduct, subject to tests like reliance, no benefit, proportionality, inextricably linked, and public
conscience, with exceptions including public interest and victimless crimes.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://lawbhoomi.com/parties-in-torts-capacity-
to-sue-and-be-sued/

XII. Capacity in tort law refers to the legal status of a person to sue or to be sued for violation of law.
Although, as a general rule, all persons may sue or be sued in tort, this is not absolute and is
subject to reasonable restrictions. Indian law largely follows English tort principles on disabilities
of parties. Parties to torts include plaintiffs (who initiate proceedings) and defendants (who
defend), and only those having the right to control proceedings or appeal are true parties; others
are privies. Proper joinder of parties is vital, as suing the wrong party or misjoinder/non-joinder
may weaken the plaintiffs case.
Certain persons face limitations in being sued or suing. Traditionally, married women could not
sue or be sued alone due to the common-law unity of spouses, but this disability was removed by
reforms like the Married Women’s Property Act, enabling independent suits. Minors can be sued
for torts like assault, defamation, fraud, etc., but may be exempt where intention or knowledge is
essential, as in Walmsey v. Humonick. Governments and municipalities may avoid liability for
acts done in discharge of sovereign functions, though liability may arise when the act is connected
with assigned duties, as in U.O.I. v. Sugrabai. A lunatic cannot be sued for acts done while not ina
stable state of mind. Alien enemies cannot be sued or sue without Central Government
permission. Corporations, having separate legal personality, can sue and be sued; however,
liability depends on whether the servant acted within authority, as illustrated in Poulton v.
London and S.W. Rly. Co. Foreign sovereigns and ambassadors enjoy immunity unless consent
and jurisdictional submission exist.
Joint tortfeasors are persons who aid, counsel, direct, or join in committing a wrongful act,
creating joint or joint-and-several responsibility. Contribution allows a tortfeasor who pays more
than his share to recover from others. Indian courts have approached English common law
cautiously; in Khushro S. Gandhi v. Guzdar, the Supreme Court held that release of all joint
tortfeasors requires full satisfaction. Joint liability commonly arises through agency, vicarious
liability, and joint action. Ex turpi causa non oritur actio bars claims arising from unlawful
conduct, subject to tests like reliance, no benefit, proportionality, inextricably linked, and public
conscience, with exceptions including public interest and victimless crimes.

to-sue-and-be-sued/

Four friends plan a violent prank and jointly push a cyclist off the road, causing serious injuries.
The cyclist sues only one friend, K, who then pays the entire damages under a settlement. K later
sues the other three friends seeking reimbursement of their shares, arguing they all participated
and should contribute. The other friends argue K paid voluntarily and cannot recover anything.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
K can recover from the others because contribution allows a tortfeasor who pays more than his
share to recover.

K cannot recover because a person who settles a claim is always treated as solely responsible
for the injury.

K can recover only if the cyclist had sued all four together; otherwise contribution is barred
completely.

K cannot recover because joint responsibility means only the plaintiff can sue, not a tortfeasor
seeking sharing.

XIII. A High Court is the highest judicial authority within a State or a group of States and Union
Territories, ranking below the Supreme Court of India and above all subordinate courts. High
Courts are not merely appellate bodies; they function as constitutional courts entrusted with
protecting rights, interpreting laws, supervising subordinate judiciary, and ensuring that
legislative and executive actions conform to constitutional principles.
India follows a single integrated judicial system, consisting of the Supreme Court, High Courts,
and subordinate courts. This system ensures uniform interpretation and application of both
Central and State laws across the country. Articles 214 to 231 of the Constitution, contained in
Part VI, govern the establishment, composition, jurisdiction, and administration of High Courts.
Parliament may establish a common High Court for multiple States or Union Territories, as
permitted by the Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956.
Each High Court consists of a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President may
determine. Judges are appointed by the President under Article 217, following consultation with
the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State, and the Chief Justice of the concerned High
Court. Judicial interpretation through the Second and Third Judges Cases has established the

primacy of the judiciary via the collegium system. A High Court judge must be an Indian citizen
and must have either ten years’ judicial experience or ten years’ practice as an advocate. Judges
hold office until the age of 62 and may be removed only through impeachment on grounds of
proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
High Courts exercise wide jurisdiction. Their original jurisdiction includes writ petitions, election
disputes, and certain civil and revenue matters. Under Article 226, High Courts may issue writs
not only for fundamental rights but also for other legal rights, giving them broader writ
jurisdiction than the Supreme Court. They primarily function as appellate courts in civil and
criminal matters and exercise supervisory control over subordinate courts under Article 227.
High Courts are Courts of Record, with binding precedents and contempt powers. They also
exercise judicial review over State and Central laws and executive actions. Constitutional
safeguards such as secure tenure, protected service conditions, and financial independence ensure
the autonomy and impartiality of High Courts, reinforcing their vital role in India’s constitutional
framework.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https:// https://www.sci.gov.in/

XIV. Protection of invention refers to the legal mechanism through which an inventor is granted
exclusive rights over their creation, preventing unauthorised making, use, sale, or distribution.
Such protection ensures recognition and financial reward for inventors while promoting innovation
and technological advancement. In India, inventions are primarily protected through patent law,
though trademarks, copyrights, industrial designs, and trade secrets may also apply depending on
the nature of the invention.
Protecting an invention is essential as it encourages innovation by assuring inventors that their
efforts will be safeguarded. Exclusive rights allow inventors to control commercial use, attract
investment, build brand value, and contribute to economic growth. Legal protection also ensures
fair recognition by preventing misuse or copying of original ideas.
Patents are the most effective method of protecting inventions. A patent is a statutory right
granted for a new invention involving an inventive step and industrial applicability, governed by
the Patents Act, 1970. Patent protection generally lasts for 20 years from the filing date. To be
patentable, an invention must be novel, non-obvious, industrially applicable, and not fall within
exclusions under Sections 3 and 4 of the Act.
The patent process involves conducting a prior art search, drafting a provisional or complete
application, filing with the Patent Office, publication, examination, response to objections, and

The invention is patentable if it is useful in business, regardless of whether it is obvious to

SECTION IV
XV. The Supreme Court has remarked that it is high time the Commission for Air Quality
Management (CAQM) realized that inordinate delay in finding solutions to worsening Air Quality
Index (AQI) will lead to further complications. The court issued directions to identify causes as
well as their long-term solutions, highlighting that the statutory expert body was asked to revisit
measures to address issues highlighted in previous orders. The Amicus Curiae has highlighted
issues like vehicular pollution with the suggestion that to curb and minimize it, steps like
transition to electric vehicles, a push for public transport, and improved enforcement like
Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) are essential.
For industrial pollution, solutions like fuel transition and emission standards have been
suggested, alongside compliance with Solid Waste Management Rules. The report also highlighted
issues like road and construction dust, firecrackers, and crop residue burning. The judiciary has
been taking up the matter from time to time, issuing directions based on expert reports. However,
the persistence of the crisis underscores a gap between judicial mandate and executive
enforcement. The need of the hour includes effective mass transport systems to limit the number
of vehicles, stringent and corruption-free pollution control norms, and re-arranging timings of
offices and educational institutions. These are not merely administrative adjustments but
essential components of environmental rule of law necessary to contain degradation.
Source: Excerpted and adapted from Down To Earth and Supreme Court proceedings coverage
(January 2026).

XVI. In December 2025, a new conversation about work-life balance started in the Indian Parliament
with the introduction of the "Right to Disconnect Bill." This private member’s bill aims to give
employees the legal right to ignore work-related calls, emails, and messages after their official
working hours end. The goal is to protect workers from the "always-on" culture that has become
common in the digital age, where smartphones turn homes into 24/7 offices. The bill proposes
setting up an Employees’ Welfare Authority to enforce these rules and requires companies with
more than 10 employees to clearly define when a workday starts and ends. However, many
business leaders are worried about how this would work in reality. They argue that in sectors like
IT, consulting, and startups, flexibility is key to competing globally. If Indian companies cannot
respond to international clients immediately because of strict "disconnect" laws, they might lose
business to other countries. There is also a fear that such rigid rules could backfire, leading
employers to micromanage workers during office hours to make up for lost time. While the bill is
unlikely to become a law immediately, it has successfully forced a national debate on mental
health and the blurring lines between our personal and professional lives.
Source: Based on analysis of the Right to Disconnect Bill, 2025 from The Times of India.

XVII. The summer of 2025 served as a severe wake-up call for India's Himalayan states, exposing the
dark side of unchecked travel. Popular destinations like Manali, Mussoorie, and Shimla faced a
crisis known as "overtourism," where the sheer volume of visitors far exceeded what the local
environment and infrastructure could support. Reports from Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh
described a chaotic scene: tourists were stuck in gridlocked traffic for hours on fragile mountain
roads, while local residents faced acute shortages of water and electricity. The surge in visitors has
pushed these "carrying capacities"—the maximum population a region can sustain without
collapsing—to their breaking point.
This crisis is not merely an inconvenience for holidaymakers; it is an environmental disaster in
the making. To cater to the rush, there has been a frenzy of unregulated construction, with hotels
and guesthouses springing up on unstable slopes. This haphazard development blocks natural
drainage paths, significantly increasing the risk of landslides and flash floods during the monsoon.
Critics argue that state governments have historically prioritized revenue over regulation,
focusing on collecting tourism taxes while ignoring the mounting waste management crisis. The
mountains are now littered with plastic and debris that local municipalities simply cannot process.
In response, experts are calling for a radical shift in how we manage hill tourism. New policy
suggestions include implementing a "green tax" or an entry permit system to limit vehicle

numbers in sensitive zones. There is also a push to promote "off-beat" rural tourism to disperse
crowds away from congested hubs. However, unless strict limits are enforced, India risks
destroying the very serenity and natural beauty that draw millions to the Himalayas in the first
place.
Source: Analysis based on The Geostrata and National Herald reports on Himalayan overtourism
(2025)

XVIII. In a major move to combat lifestyle diseases, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
(FSSAI) has introduced tougher rules for food labeling in 2025, fundamentally changing how
packaged food is sold. The most significant update is the mandatory "Front-of-Pack Labeling"
(FOPL) for items classified as High in Fat, Salt, and Sugar (HFSS). Previously, nutritional
information was buried in tiny, unreadable text on the back of the packet. The new norms require
this critical data to be displayed boldly on the front, acting as an immediate warning to
consumers. This shift is designed to help buyers make healthier choices instantly, without needing
a degree in nutrition to understand the ingredients list. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The regulations also target the misleading "health halo" that many brands use to sell processed
foods. For instance, if a company claims its cookies are "rich in protein" or "zero cholesterol," they
must now provide laboratory-verified proof to back up these assertions. The FSSAI has set a strict
timeline, with a compliance deadline of July 1, 2025, for companies to update their packaging.
This has caused some friction in the industry, with manufacturers arguing that changing labels is
expensive and that the new warning symbols might "demonize" traditional Indian snacks.
However, health experts argue that these strict measures are necessary because India is rapidly
becoming the "diabetes capital" of the world. By forcing transparency, the government aims to
shift the responsibility back to the manufacturers. Furthermore, even restaurant chains and
online food delivery apps are now required to display calorie counts for their dishes, ensuring that
consumers are aware of what they are eating, whether they are cooking at home or ordering in.
Source: Expanded analysis based on FSSAI’s 2025 Nutrition Labelling Amendment coverage by
Envirocare Labs.

(FSSAI) has introduced tougher rules for food labeling in 2025, fundamentally changing how
packaged food is sold. The most significant update is the mandatory "Front-of-Pack Labeling"
(FOPL) for items classified as High in Fat, Salt, and Sugar (HFSS). Previously, nutritional
information was buried in tiny, unreadable text on the back of the packet. The new norms require
this critical data to be displayed boldly on the front, acting as an immediate warning to
consumers. This shift is designed to help buyers make healthier choices instantly, without needing
a degree in nutrition to understand the ingredients list. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The regulations also target the misleading "health halo" that many brands use to sell processed
foods. For instance, if a company claims its cookies are "rich in protein" or "zero cholesterol," they
must now provide laboratory-verified proof to back up these assertions. The FSSAI has set a strict
timeline, with a compliance deadline of July 1, 2025, for companies to update their packaging.
This has caused some friction in the industry, with manufacturers arguing that changing labels is
expensive and that the new warning symbols might "demonize" traditional Indian snacks.
However, health experts argue that these strict measures are necessary because India is rapidly
becoming the "diabetes capital" of the world. By forcing transparency, the government aims to
shift the responsibility back to the manufacturers. Furthermore, even restaurant chains and
online food delivery apps are now required to display calorie counts for their dishes, ensuring that
consumers are aware of what they are eating, whether they are cooking at home or ordering in.
Source: Expanded analysis based on FSSAI’s 2025 Nutrition Labelling Amendment coverage by
Envirocare Labs.

I.	It was a wonderful night, such a night as is only possible when we are young, dear reader. The sky
was so starry, so bright that, looking at it, one could not help asking oneself whether ill-humoured
and capricious people could live under such a sky. That is a youthful question too, dear reader,
very youthful, but may the Lord put it more frequently into your heart.
From early morning I had been oppressed by a strange despondency. It suddenly seemed to me
that I was lonely, that everyone was forsaking me and going away from me. For though I had been
living almost eight years in Petersburg I had hardly an acquaintance. But what did I want with
acquaintances? I was acquainted with all Petersburg as it was; that was why I felt as though they
were all deserting me when all Petersburg packed up and went to its summer villa.
I know the houses too. As I walk along they seem to run forward in the streets to look out at me
from every window, and almost to say: “Good-morning! How do you do? I am quite well, thank
God, and I am to have a new storey in May,” or, “How are you? I am being redecorated to-morrow;”
or, “I was almost burnt down and had such a fright,” and so on. I have my favourites among them,
some are dear friends. One of them intends to be treated by the architect this summer. I shall go
every day on purpose to see that the operation is not a failure.
Source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, White Nights, “First Night”, in White Nights and Other Stories, trans.

was so starry, so bright that, looking at it, one could not help asking oneself whether ill-humoured
and capricious people could live under such a sky. That is a youthful question too, dear reader,
very youthful, but may the Lord put it more frequently into your heart.
From early morning I had been oppressed by a strange despondency. It suddenly seemed to me
that I was lonely, that everyone was forsaking me and going away from me. For though I had been
living almost eight years in Petersburg I had hardly an acquaintance. But what did I want with
acquaintances? I was acquainted with all Petersburg as it was; that was why I felt as though they
were all deserting me when all Petersburg packed up and went to its summer villa.
I know the houses too. As I walk along they seem to run forward in the streets to look out at me
from every window, and almost to say: “Good-morning! How do you do? I am quite well, thank
God, and I am to have a new storey in May,” or, “How are you? I am being redecorated to-morrow;”
or, “I was almost burnt down and had such a fright,” and so on. I have my favourites among them,
some are dear friends. One of them intends to be treated by the architect this summer. I shall go
every day on purpose to see that the operation is not a failure.

Il.	The house had grown old in its silence, like a woman aging without the grace of youth. Eleanor
pushed open the creaking door, her lantern casting trembling shadows against the walls. The air
tasted of dust and forgotten time. She had come searching for her sister, who had vanished three
weeks prior under circumstances that the town preferred not to discuss. The locals called the
mansion "cursed," but Eleanor knew better—curses were merely explanations for things people
could not understand. The servants had long abandoned their posts; the kitchen held no warmth.
In the parlor, she found a leather journal, its pages yellowed and brittle. The handwriting within
was frantic, documenting observations of something that moved through the halls after dark,
something that whispered her sister's name. The entries grew increasingly incoherent, the
author's fear palpable in every crossed-out word. Eleanor's hands trembled as she read by
candlelight. The final entry was dated the night her sister disappeared: "It knows me now. It calls,
and I must answer." What Eleanor discovered next would haunt her forever—a door beneath the
stairs, previously invisible, now standing ajar. Behind it lay nothing but an impenetrable darkness
and the faint echo of a familiar voice calling her name.
Source: A Whisper at Midnight; Book by Darcy Burke

Il. Dr. Harish Verma had spent thirty years pursuing a solution that existed only in his mind. The
numbers had begun to speak to him at university, whispering patterns that others could not hear.
His colleagues dismissed his theories as eccentricities, the harmless obsessions of a gifted mind.
But Harish knew the truth: he had discovered something that transcended conventional
mathematics, a formula that explained the fundamental relationship between chaos and order in
the universe. He had isolated himself in his study, surrounding himself with notebooks filled with
calculations that no peer reviewer would ever accept. His wife had left him a decade ago, unable to
reconcile the man who recited equations in his sleep with the man she had married. His daughter
stopped visiting. The world outside his study had become irrelevant, a distraction from work that
consumed every waking moment. One evening, reviewing his life's work, Harish realized
something horrifying: every formula, every carefully derived proof, had been constructed within
the fortress of his own mind. There existed no means of validation, no experiment that could test
his claims, no evidence that distinguished his discovery from elaborate hallucination. In that
moment of clarity, he understood that genius and madness might be separated only by the
thinnest of lines, and that he may have crossed it long ago without ever realizing when the
crossing occurred.

content.passageText:
IV.	The garden had belonged to the Chowdhury family for seven generations, a small plot of earth in
Mumbai where jasmine vines climbed white walls and crows nested in the old neem tree. Maya
returned to it after fifteen years of living abroad, expecting nostalgia. Instead, she found
bewilderment. Everything was smaller than she remembered—the garden she had imagined as
vast now seemed confined, almost suffocating in its smallness. Her grandfather sat in the
courtyard as he always had, though age had rendered him nearly unrecognizable. His hands, once
strong enough to coax blooms from stubborn soil, trembled as he tended the plants. He did not
acknowledge her arrival; perhaps he did not recognize her. Maya wandered through the garden,
touching the familiar plants, and noticed something strange: the flowers were blooming in the
wrong season, their colors muted and peculiar. The gardener, old Ranjit, spoke to her in hushed
tones that evening. He told her that her grandfather had not spoken a word in three years, that he
spent every night under the neem tree, whispering to the darkness. Ranjit believed the garden
was dying, that something fundamental had shifted in the earth itself. When Maya finally
approached her grandfather to embrace him, he recoiled. As she stood there, rejected and
bewildered, she understood that she had lost not just the garden of her childhood but the
grandfather she thought she knew.
Source: The Secret Garden; Novel by Frances Hodgson Burnett

returned to it after fifteen years of living abroad, expecting nostalgia. Instead, she found
bewilderment. Everything was smaller than she remembered—the garden she had imagined as
vast now seemed confined, almost suffocating in its smallness. Her grandfather sat in the
courtyard as he always had, though age had rendered him nearly unrecognizable. His hands, once
strong enough to coax blooms from stubborn soil, trembled as he tended the plants. He did not
acknowledge her arrival; perhaps he did not recognize her. Maya wandered through the garden,
touching the familiar plants, and noticed something strange: the flowers were blooming in the
wrong season, their colors muted and peculiar. The gardener, old Ranjit, spoke to her in hushed
tones that evening. He told her that her grandfather had not spoken a word in three years, that he
spent every night under the neem tree, whispering to the darkness. Ranjit believed the garden
was dying, that something fundamental had shifted in the earth itself. When Maya finally
approached her grandfather to embrace him, he recoiled. As she stood there, rejected and
bewildered, she understood that she had lost not just the garden of her childhood but the
grandfather she thought she knew.
Source: The Secret Garden; Novel by Frances Hodgson Burnett

settled in the Ratanmahal Wildlife Sanctuary in Dahod district. Tigers had become extinct in the

VII. In October 2025, a landmark United Nations treaty addressing cybercrime was opened for
signature by member states in Hanoi, Viet Nam, marking a significant step in global cooperation
on digital security. The agreement represents the first universal framework designed to
strengthen collective defences against cybercrime by criminalising a range of offences and
facilitating cross-border cooperation among law enforcement agencies. It seeks to respond to the
expanding misuse of information and communication technologies, which enable activities such as
online fraud, financial crime, human trafficking, and other serious offences. A central feature of
the treaty is the creation of mechanisms for the collection, sharing and use of electronic evidence
across jurisdictions, as well as the establishment of a network to support rapid international
collaboration. The convention also emphasises capacity building and technical assistance,
particularly for countries with limited resources to address complex digital threats. By providing a
legally binding instrument for coordinated action, the treaty aims to enhance global preparedness
and response to cybercrime while supporting the rule of law and protection of citizens in an
increasingly interconnected world.

VIII. The Nazi regime made systematic and strategic use of language and media to advance its ideology
and consolidate public support. Official communications deliberately avoided direct words such as
“kill” or “murder,” replacing them with misleading and euphemistic terms that concealed the
reality of mass violence. Expressions like “special treatment,” “final solution” for Jews,
“euthanasia” for the disabled, and “selection” or “disinfection” were employed to normalise and
obscure acts of killing. Deportations to gas chambers were referred to as “evacuations,” while the
gas chambers themselves were labelled “disinfection areas” and designed to resemble bathrooms
with fake showerheads, further masking their true purpose.
Alongside this manipulation of language, the regime used media extensively to popularise its
worldview. Visual imagery, films, radio broadcasts, posters, slogans, and leaflets were used to
spread Nazi ideas and shape public opinion. Groups identified as enemies of the state were
stereotyped, mocked, and portrayed as dangerous or evil. Socialists and liberals were depicted as
weak and corrupt, while Jews were systematically dehumanised through propaganda, most
notably in films such as *The Eternal Jew*. These portrayals aimed to inflame emotions, redirect
public anger, and legitimise persecution of those labelled as “undesirable.”
Source: Excerpts from NCERT History Textbook, Class IX, India and the Contemporary World — I,
Chapter: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler, National Council of Educational Research and Training,
New Dethi

content.questionText:
According to the passage, what is the primary distinction between the "retrospective" and
"retroactive" application of a law?
options:
Retrospective application only affects future events, while retroactive application changes past
laws.

Retrospective application changes the legal consequences of past acts, while retroactive
application imposes new burdens on a continuing state of affairs that began in the past.

Retrospective application is permitted under Article 20(1), whereas retroactive application is
strictly prohibited.

There is no distinction; both terms refer to criminalizing an act that was legal when it was
committed.

XI.	In the landmark judgment of State of UP v. Ajmal Beg, the Supreme Court of India expressed
grave concern over the "institutionalized evil" of dowry, which persists despite legal prohibitions.
The Bench observed that dowry has morphed from a voluntary practice intended for a woman's
financial independence into a mechanism for material extraction. The Court emphasized that this
practice is fundamentally at odds with the constitutional values of justice, liberty, and fraternity,
directly violating Article 14’s guarantee of equality by treating women as sources of financial gain.
The case involved the dowry death of a 20-year-old woman, married for just over a year, who was
subjected to persistent demands for a motorcycle, electronics, and cash. While the Allahabad High
Court had previously acquitted the accused—reasoning that their poverty made such demands
improbable—the Supreme Court set aside this acquittal. The Bench clarified that the Dowry
Prohibition Act makes no distinction between demands made before or after marriage and
asserted that financial status does not negate the probability of dowry harassment. Consequently,
the conviction of the husband and his mother was restored, though the Court refrained from
incarcerating the 94-year-old mother-in-law due to her age.
Significantly, the Court noted that dowry is a systemic issue prevalent across all religions in the
subcontinent. It observed that in some communities, dowry has been adopted alongside nominal
religious gifts like mehr, hollowing out the original protective purpose of such customs. To address
this social conditioning, the Court issued a series of directives, including:
Incorporating constitutional values of equality into educational curricula.
Ensuring the effective appointment and visibility of Dowry Prohibition Officers.
Sensitizing police and judicial officers to the psychological dimensions of dowry cases.
Expediting long-pending trials under Sections 304B (dowry death) and 498A (cruelty) of the IPC.
Ultimately, the Court underscored that true independence necessitates social transformation,
urging authorities to eradicate entrenched customs that undermine the dignity and financial
security of women.

XII. In the law of torts, liability is typically categorized as either fault-based or no-fault. Under no-fault
liability, a defendant is held accountable for damages even in the absence of negligence or intent.
This concept is divided into two primary doctrines: Strict Liability and Absolute Liability.
Strict Liability was established in the landmark English case Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). It
dictates that if a person brings onto their land anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, they
are prima facie liable for any damage caused by its escape, regardless of how much care was
taken. For this rule to apply, three essentials must be met: the defendant must bring a hazardous
substance onto their property, there must be a "non-natural" use of the land, and the substance
must actually escape the premises and cause harm.
However, Strict Liability is not an exhaustive rule and provides some specific defenses:
1. Plaintiffs Own Fault: If the damage resulted from the plaintiff's own trespassing or
negligence.

2. Act of God: Unforeseeable and uncontrollable natural disasters.
8. Volenti Non-Fit Injuria: If the dangerous substance was maintained for the mutual benefit of
both parties.
4. Act of a Stranger: If a third party over whom the defendant had no control caused the escape.
5. Statutory Authority: If the act was performed under the mandate of law.
Absolute Liability is a more stringent Indian legal doctrine evolved by the Supreme Court in M.C.
Mehta v. Union of India. Prompted by the 1984 Bhopal Gas Tragedy, the Court realized that the
traditional exceptions to Strict Liability allowed hazardous industries to evade accountability for
mass disasters. This rule states that an enterprise engaged in an inherently dangerous or
hazardous activity is liable for any harm resulting from an accident during that activity. Unlike
the Rylands rule, Absolute Liability is not subject to any exceptions; the defendant cannot escape
liability by claiming an Act of God or the act of a stranger. This ensures that high-risk industries
bear the full cost of any danger they introduce into society.

This concept is divided into two primary doctrines: Strict Liability and Absolute Liability.
Strict Liability was established in the landmark English case Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). It
dictates that if a person brings onto their land anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, they
are prima facie liable for any damage caused by its escape, regardless of how much care was
taken. For this rule to apply, three essentials must be met: the defendant must bring a hazardous
substance onto their property, there must be a "non-natural" use of the land, and the substance
must actually escape the premises and cause harm.
However, Strict Liability is not an exhaustive rule and provides some specific defenses:
1. Plaintiffs Own Fault: If the damage resulted from the plaintiff's own trespassing or
negligence.

2. Act of God: Unforeseeable and uncontrollable natural disasters.
8. Volenti Non-Fit Injuria: If the dangerous substance was maintained for the mutual benefit of
both parties.
4. Act of a Stranger: If a third party over whom the defendant had no control caused the escape.
5. Statutory Authority: If the act was performed under the mandate of law.
Absolute Liability is a more stringent Indian legal doctrine evolved by the Supreme Court in M.C.
Mehta v. Union of India. Prompted by the 1984 Bhopal Gas Tragedy, the Court realized that the
traditional exceptions to Strict Liability allowed hazardous industries to evade accountability for
mass disasters. This rule states that an enterprise engaged in an inherently dangerous or
hazardous activity is liable for any harm resulting from an accident during that activity. Unlike

liability by claiming an Act of God or the act of a stranger. This ensures that high-risk industries
bear the full cost of any danger they introduce into society.

XIII. The Indian Constitution is anchored by a triad of fundamental provisions collectively known as
the "Golden Triangle": Articles 14, 19, and 21. Rather than existing as isolated legal mandates,
these articles form an interconnected web that serves as the ultimate bulwark against arbitrary
state action and the primary protector of individual dignity. The concept of the Golden Triangle
emphasizes that these rights are mutually reinforcing; the deprivation of one often leads to the
erosion of the others.
Article 14 establishes the foundational principle of equality, guaranteeing "equality before the
law" and "equal protection of the laws." It prohibits the State from discriminating on grounds such
as religion, race, caste, or sex. Landmark rulings, such as Keshavananda Bharati (1973), have
recognized this right to equality as part of the Constitution's "basic structure," meaning it cannot
be abrogated even by constitutional amendments.
Article 19 delineates the essential freedoms of a citizen, including speech, assembly, movement,
and profession. While these freedoms are vital for a functional democracy, they are not absolute.
The State may impose "reasonable restrictions" on grounds like national security or public order.
However, as established in Romesh Thappar (1950), the threshold for these restrictions is high,
ensuring that even unpopular critiques of the government remain protected.
Article 21is the most evolved provision, safeguarding the right to life and personal liberty.
Initially interpreted narrowly, the landmark Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) case

fundamentally transformed its scope. The Court ruled that any "procedure established by law"
used to deprive a person of liberty must not be arbitrary, but must be "just, fair, and
reasonable." This decision effectively synthesized the three articles, holding that a law under
Article 21 must also pass the tests of Article 14 (non-arbitrariness) and Article 19
(reasonableness).
The interdependence of the Triangle is best seen in modern judicial expansions, where the "right
to life" now encompasses the right to privacy (Puttaswamy), a clean environment, and even
emergency medical care. A notable application is the "Golden Hour" principle, where the judiciary
linked Article 21 to the mandatory duty of healthcare providers to treat accident victims, ensuring
that dignity and life are prioritized over procedural formalities.
Ultimately, the Golden Triangle represents the democratic essence of India. It ensures that the
administration of justice is not merely a matter of following rules, but a commitment to upholding
a triad of values—equality, freedom, and dignity—that are indispensable to the human
experience.

Race, Caste, Profession, Sex, and Religion.

XIV. On July 1, 2024, India transitioned from its colonial-era criminal justice framework to a modern,
indigenous system with the enforcement of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya
Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA). These laws
replaced the Indian Penal Code (1860), the Code of Criminal Procedure (1973), and the Indian
Evidence Act (1872), respectively. A central theme of this overhaul is the "decolonization" of law
and the integration of technology into the judicial process.
Under the BNSS, procedural efficiency has been prioritized through mandated timelines. For
instance, Section 173 of the BNSS mandates that a preliminary inquiry must be conducted within
14 days in cases punishable with 3 to 7 years of imprisonment. Furthermore, the law now allows
for the registration of a "Zero FIR" at any police station, regardless of the area of jurisdiction,
ensuring that victims are not turned away due to territorial technicalities. The BNS has also
redefined several offenses. Notably, "Sedition" (formerly Section 124A of the IPC) has been
replaced by Section 152, which penalizes "acts endangering sovereignty, unity, and integrity of
India." Unlike the old law, Section 152 explicitly excludes "comments made in good faith or in a

reasonable manner" regarding government action, focusing instead on secessionist activities or
armed rebellion.
Crucially, the BSA has expanded the definition of evidence. Under Section 61 of the BSA,
electronic or digital records are now categorized as "primary evidence," whereas they were
previously often treated as secondary evidence requiring stringent certification. In a 2025 ruling,
the Supreme Court clarified that while electronic evidence is primary, the procedural safeguards
under the BSA—such as ensuring the integrity of the storage device—must be strictly followed to
prevent tampering. The Court noted that the transition to the new laws is "prospective," meaning
crimes committed before July 1, 2024, will continue to be tried under the old IPC/CrPC, while new
offenses fall under the BNS/BNSS.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from The Criminal Law Reform Analysis, November
2025

The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), as it governs the trial procedure.
The Indian Penal Code (IPC), because the transition to the new laws is prospective.

content.passageText:
XVI. India's Urban Mobility Crisis: India stands at a critical crossroads. Its urban centers are
growing rapidly with more people buying private vehicles, creating severe traffic congestion, air
pollution, and a declining quality of life. This crisis did not happen by accident—it is the direct
result of decades of planning that prioritized cars over public transportation. Most Indian cities
have focused heavily on building metro rail systems while neglecting buses and other transport
modes. This "one size fits all" approach has created serious problems: areas without metro
coverage have almost no transit options, forcing people to buy cars and motorcycles.
The real issue is that governments have been moving cars, not people. A city like Bengaluru has
more buses per mile than most cities, yet it performs poorly compared to international standards
because it lacks good last-mile connectivity and pedestrian-friendly streets. Projects like tunnel
roads and coastal highways seem smart temporarily because they reduce traffic, but they
ultimately invite more vehicles onto the roads—a phenomenon called "induced demand."
Meanwhile, cities are destroying valuable public spaces for these projects without solving the
actual problem. www.lawpreptutorial.com
However, there are positive signs. Survey data shows that most people are willing to use quality
public transportation if available. Metro systems are expanding rapidly, and some cities are
redesigning streets with wide pedestrian paths. Bengaluru plans to deploy 10,000 buses in coming
years. For real progress, citizens must demand better urban planning from their governments and
choose public transit over personal vehicles. Only a fundamental mindset shift from "moving cars"
to "moving people" can create the liveable cities India needs.
Source: The Journal Club (Bit News), September 2025; India's Urban Mobility Crisis

Governments have consistently prioritized expanding road infrastructure for cars over people-

infrastructure across cities.
content.explanation: The passage explicitly identifies car prioritization as the core cause of the crisis.

XVI. India's Urban Mobility Crisis: India stands at a critical crossroads. Its urban centers are
growing rapidly with more people buying private vehicles, creating severe traffic congestion, air
pollution, and a declining quality of life. This crisis did not happen by accident—it is the direct
result of decades of planning that prioritized cars over public transportation. Most Indian cities
have focused heavily on building metro rail systems while neglecting buses and other transport
modes. This "one size fits all" approach has created serious problems: areas without metro
coverage have almost no transit options, forcing people to buy cars and motorcycles.
The real issue is that governments have been moving cars, not people. A city like Bengaluru has
more buses per mile than most cities, yet it performs poorly compared to international standards
because it lacks good last-mile connectivity and pedestrian-friendly streets. Projects like tunnel
roads and coastal highways seem smart temporarily because they reduce traffic, but they
ultimately invite more vehicles onto the roads—a phenomenon called "induced demand."
Meanwhile, cities are destroying valuable public spaces for these projects without solving the
actual problem. www.lawpreptutorial.com
However, there are positive signs. Survey data shows that most people are willing to use quality
public transportation if available. Metro systems are expanding rapidly, and some cities are
redesigning streets with wide pedestrian paths. Bengaluru plans to deploy 10,000 buses in coming
years. For real progress, citizens must demand better urban planning from their governments and
choose public transit over personal vehicles. Only a fundamental mindset shift from "moving cars"
to "moving people" can create the liveable cities India needs.
Source: The Journal Club (Bit News), September 2025; India's Urban Mobility Crisis

content.passageText:
XVII. India's Employability Crisis: India produces over 3 million graduates annually, yet only about
half are considered employable by industry standards. This creates a paradox: thousands of
educated young people remain unemployed while companies struggle to find skilled workers. The
problem is not a shortage of graduates but a fundamental mismatch between what students learn
and what employers need. Engineering and commerce graduates often end up working as clerks or
machine operators—roles that don't require their qualifications—because they lack practical
experience and industry exposure.
The education system emphasizes rote learning and memorization for exams rather than
developing critical thinking and communication skills. Employers consistently report that only
50% of graduates can handle communication-based roles effectively, and merely 44% demonstrate
adequate creative thinking ability. Young people graduate with theoretical knowledge but cannot
solve real-world problems. Additionally, gender and geography create barriers: male graduates
show 43.4% employability compared to 41.7% for females, and Delhi leads at 53.4% employability
while states like Uttar Pradesh and Assam lag significantly behind.
Government initiatives like Skill India and the National Education Policy 2020 promise
improvements, but implementation remains patchy. Private companies offer training programs,
but these mostly benefit students from top-tier colleges. Until curriculum reforms prioritize skill
development, internship programs expand significantly, and training scales across all regions and
social groups, educated unemployment will persist. The solution requires not just more jobs but
fundamental education system transformation aligned with actual industry needs.
Source: India Today Education, India Skills Report 2026, November 2025

XVIII. Facial Recognition and Digital Privacy Concerns: As artificial intelligence advances, facial
recognition technology has become increasingly powerful and accessible. Governments and private
companies can now identify individuals in crowds, track movement patterns, and monitor
behaviour with minimal human oversight. This creates unprecedented privacy risks. Consider
what happens when facial recognition is used without consent at airports, shopping malls, or
public protests: individuals lose the ability to move through public spaces anonymously. In
authoritarian regimes, this technology enables mass surveillance systems that suppress dissent
and control populations. Even in democracies, the absence of clear consent mechanisms means
people cannot opt out of being scanned and tracked.
The core problem is that current regulations lag far behind the technology's capabilities. Data
protection laws often require consent before collecting personal information, but facial recognition
systems operate silently and invisibly. A person walking down the street has no way to know if
their face has been captured, analyzed, and stored in a database. This asymmetry of power—
where authorities can watch citizens but citizens cannot know they are being watched—
undermines the basic principles of democratic society. Facial recognition technology also amplifies
bias: studies show that these systems are significantly less accurate for people with darker skin
tones, creating disparities in both surveillance and error rates.
Addressing this crisis requires explicit legal protections: banning facial recognition in sensitive
contexts like protests and public spaces, requiring transparent reporting of surveillance activities,
and building independent oversight mechanisms to review government access to biometric data.
Without strong regulatory action, facial recognition will become a tool for unchecked state and
corporate power, fundamentally changing the relationship between individuals and institutions.
Source: Online, December 2025 & OHCHR Joint Declaration on AI

SECTION I
I.	The theory of natural selection, as articulated by Charles Darwin and independently
formulated by Alfred Russel Wallace, is often celebrated not merely for its originality but for
its decisive explanatory economy. What distinguishes it from earlier speculative accounts of
life is its capacity to resolve, with remarkable conceptual restraint, the long-standing puzzle of
purposiveness in nature. Where earlier frameworks were compelled to invoke design or pre-
established harmony to account for the precise adaptation of organisms to their environments,
the principle of selection renders such assumptions not only unnecessary but intellectually
excessive.
Darwin’s insight did not emerge fully formed but was preceded by a careful engagement with
the problem of variability. Observing how human breeders selectively amplified desirable
traits, he recognised that transformation within species required no mysterious force, only the
consistent retention of certain variations over others. Yet the critical difficulty lay in
extending this logic to nature itself, where no conscious selector appeared to operate. It is here
that Darwin’s engagement with Malthus becomes pivotal: the realisation that organisms
reproduce in excess of what their environments can sustain introduces an unavoidable
condition of competition.
This condition, which Darwin termed the “struggle for existence,” is frequently misunderstood
when reduced to crude images of predation. Its true significance lies in the far subtler and
more pervasive competition among individuals of the same species, where even marginal
advantages determine survival. The evaluative force of Darwin’s argument rests precisely on
this point: what survives is not the strongest in any absolute sense, but the most suitably
constituted relative to specific conditions. In this sense, selection is less an event than a
continuous filtration.
Such a view compels a reconsideration of adaptation itself. Rather than being evidence of prior
intention, adaptation emerges as the cumulative outcome of innumerable eliminations, where
non-advantageous variations are quietly discarded. The elegance of this explanation lies in its
refusal to posit any guiding intelligence; instead, it locates order in repetition. Over successive
generations, this repeated selection produces structures that appear purposive, though they
are nothing more than the residue of what has endured.
It is this relentless emphasis on repetition—on the continual preservation of the relatively
better suited—that constitutes the true strength of the theory. By grounding complexity in a
simple, recurring process, Darwin not only displaces earlier metaphysical explanations but
also establishes a framework within which both diversity and precision can be understood
without recourse to external design. The enduring power of natural selection lies, therefore,
not in any single insight, but in the consistency with which it explains the emergence of form
through the repeated survival of the suitable.
Source: On Darwin’s Theory of Natural Selection — explanatory scientific text

SECTION I
I.	The theory of natural selection, as articulated by Charles Darwin and independently
formulated by Alfred Russel Wallace, is often celebrated not merely for its originality but for
its decisive explanatory economy. What distinguishes it from earlier speculative accounts of
life is its capacity to resolve, with remarkable conceptual restraint, the long-standing puzzle of
purposiveness in nature. Where earlier frameworks were compelled to invoke design or pre-
established harmony to account for the precise adaptation of organisms to their environments,
the principle of selection renders such assumptions not only unnecessary but intellectually
excessive.
Darwin’s insight did not emerge fully formed but was preceded by a careful engagement with
the problem of variability. Observing how human breeders selectively amplified desirable
traits, he recognised that transformation within species required no mysterious force, only the
consistent retention of certain variations over others. Yet the critical difficulty lay in
extending this logic to nature itself, where no conscious selector appeared to operate. It is here
that Darwin’s engagement with Malthus becomes pivotal: the realisation that organisms
reproduce in excess of what their environments can sustain introduces an unavoidable
condition of competition.
This condition, which Darwin termed the “struggle for existence,” is frequently misunderstood
when reduced to crude images of predation. Its true significance lies in the far subtler and
more pervasive competition among individuals of the same species, where even marginal
advantages determine survival. The evaluative force of Darwin’s argument rests precisely on
this point: what survives is not the strongest in any absolute sense, but the most suitably
constituted relative to specific conditions. In this sense, selection is less an event than a
continuous filtration.
Such a view compels a reconsideration of adaptation itself. Rather than being evidence of prior
intention, adaptation emerges as the cumulative outcome of innumerable eliminations, where
non-advantageous variations are quietly discarded. The elegance of this explanation lies in its
refusal to posit any guiding intelligence; instead, it locates order in repetition. Over successive
generations, this repeated selection produces structures that appear purposive, though they
are nothing more than the residue of what has endured.
It is this relentless emphasis on repetition—on the continual preservation of the relatively
better suited—that constitutes the true strength of the theory. By grounding complexity in a
simple, recurring process, Darwin not only displaces earlier metaphysical explanations but
also establishes a framework within which both diversity and precision can be understood
without recourse to external design. The enduring power of natural selection lies, therefore,
not in any single insight, but in the consistency with which it explains the emergence of form
through the repeated survival of the suitable.
