content.passageText:
X.	The Supreme Court recently passed a judgment in a case that has been in court since 2001,
regarding compensation for the death of a woman in a road accident. The judgment proposed
that a notional amount of Rs 30,000 be seen as a benchmark for compensation cases to
recognise the economic value of a housewife and their role as “nation builders”. Honourable as
their intentions may have been, their ascribing a “wage,” as it were, to housework is a stark
reminder of the huge gender gap in housework and care work in India. The experience of
domestic life is diverse. From a joint family to a nuclear one, to caregiving for those with
disabilities or the elderly, the textures of every household are different. Yet, common among
them is the predominance of labour done by women of the household, or by domestic workers,
often migrants, from oppressed castes and resource-poor backgrounds.
Women spend about 289 minutes a day on unpaid domestic work, as compared to men, who
spend 88 minutes, as per the national Time Use Survey 2024. The time women spend on
unpaid housework has gone down by only 10 minutes in the last seven years. Will a judgment
like this change this imbalance? Even as it acknowledges women’s household labour as having
monetary value, it does not move us away from the notion that housework is a woman’s
responsibility, that a woman’s place is in the home.
In the 1970s, the famous “Wages for Housework” campaign in the UK started by the
International Feminist Collective had a telling slogan: “They say it is love. We say it is
unwaged labour”. Demanding wages was a symbolic way to visibilise the labour women did in
the home. It was the first step to rejecting housework as only women’s work and stepping out
of the prison of unequal gender roles. Over decades, campaigns like this have asked women to
withdraw from their domestic roles for a day — a feminist strike. In the rare instances that
the feminist strike has been deployed, it has shaken the earth.
Absence, as we learnt in the pandemic of domestic workers, creates value. It was the death of
the woman in the motor accident that underpins the recent judgment. To be recognised for
your “worth” after you are dead is an irony, but for those who are living, is this really what
they want? www.lawpreptutorial.com
The demand from feminists has never been only “wages for housework”. It is for recognition of
unpaid housework as women’s labour, a burden they carry disproportionately. It is for the
recognition of the value of that labour that sustains life and society. Most importantly, it is for
institutional change that redistributes this burden, in line with society’s ideals of equality and
justice. [Word Count: 460]

https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/columns /supreme-court-housewives-domestic-
workers-gender-wage-equality-10745593/

content.passageText:
XI.	Public debates about transgender issues are often framed as disagreements over evidence or
safety. In my new article published in the International Journal of Transgender Health, I
argue current policy shifts are better understood as part of a recognisable escalation pattern.
I call this “trans eliminationism” — efforts to remove trans people from social, legal or physical
existence. The concept of eliminationism was developed by political scientist Daniel Goldhagen
to describe ideologies that frame a targeted group as incompatible with society and therefore
as requiring removal.
Trans eliminationism exists on a continuum.
At the less severe end, though still deeply harmful, is social and legal erasure such as
restricting healthcare access, prohibiting changes to identity documents, removing gender as a
protected category, banning trans content from schools and libraries, and pushing trans youth
into conversion practices. Some of these measures are now occurring in many jurisdictions. For
example, across the United States, anti-trans bills continue to be introduced in various states
and in New Zealand, the Legislation (Definitions of Woman and Man) Amendment Bill is
currently open for submissions. Social and legal eliminationism can create conditions in which
more severe forms of harm, including incarceration and physical violence, become easier to
justify by weakening legal protections, normalising exclusion, and reducing the social and
political costs of further restrictions. For some of the most marginalised trans people,
incarceration and violence are already a lived reality.
Research on eliminationist movements points to recurring mechanisms through which
societies move from foundational prejudice to increasingly severe restrictions and harms. One
is dehumanisation. When a group is portrayed as irrational, defective, immoral or less
deserving of dignity, moral inhibitions about harming them are lowered. This makes it easier
to justify restrictions on their rights or to dismiss their testimony and experiences. Another is
the artificial construction of a perceived threat. Targeted groups are framed as a danger to
children, public safety or social order. This generates the urgency needed for public
mobilisation, because measures that would otherwise seem discriminatory can instead be
presented as necessary forms of protection. A third mechanism, specific to trans
eliminationism, is what I call biological reductionism. This involves reducing the complexity of
sex and gender to a single biological characteristic and treating it as a person’s essential
nature — determining who someone really is, regardless of their lived experience, social role,
body or self-understanding.
It is then used to determine how they should be recognised and treated in areas such as
healthcare, law, education and sport. Under this logic, trans people become impossible by

XII. The Amazon rainforest, according to a 2021 study, is losing its capacity as a carbon sink and
now emits more than it absorbs. In the tropics, marine scientists are reporting that coral reefs
are in decline, threatening fish stocks. Equally concerning is research into the Atlantic
Meridional Overturning Circulation (Amoc), a vast system of ocean currents that helps
regulate the climate and is at risk of collapsing this century. The entire global ecosystem
appears to be losing its ability to function.
We find this view in newspapers, magazines, technical reports and the journals of learned
societies. But thinking about the environment in terms of its functions is also how many of us
tend to understand the world. We may think that forests exist to produce oxygen, wetlands to
filter water and bees to pollinate our crops.
There is a problem with this way of thinking: ecosystems don’t exist to perform goals. The
Amazon absorbs carbon, but it doesn’t “aim” to do so. It simply exists. Any standards of
operation we find in nature have come directly from our own desires for things such as climate
stability, abundant fisheries, beauty or cultural meaning.
So why do we keep thinking ecosystems have functions they could fail to perform?
I came to this puzzle as a graduate student in the late 1990s, a time when research into
biodiversity and ecosystem function was rapidly increasing. Initially, I thought I would write
my dissertation on a conventional ecological topic: whether species richness drives
productivity. Instead, I fell in with the philosophy of science crowd, attended their seminars
and eventually earned a master’s degree in philosophy alongside my work in ecology. There I
encountered a rich debate over the concept of function — what it means, when it applies, what
work it does. But no one seemed to be connecting that debate to the way ecologists were using
the same word, unreflectively, to describe what ecosystems do. This essay is an attempt to
bring those conversations together.
My concern with ecosystems and function was never just academic. I am an environmentalist,
unsettled by the loss of natural places. And as a father, I am concerned that my generation
will leave to our children a planet depleted in both richness and resilience. These
commitments also drive my interest in debates about function. If the way we think about
ecological crisis is conceptually shaky, we risk obscuring what’s really at stake.
I worry that the ways we often conceive of the problems before us are inadequate. For if
ecosystems have no intrinsic ends and cannot truly “break down”, how do we repair them?
How do we respond to environmental crises in a world of aimless ecosystems? [Word Count:
447]

https: //www.theguardian.com/news/2026/jun/18/can-ecosystems-malfunction

content.passageText:
XII. The Amazon rainforest, according to a 2021 study, is losing its capacity as a carbon sink and
now emits more than it absorbs. In the tropics, marine scientists are reporting that coral reefs
are in decline, threatening fish stocks. Equally concerning is research into the Atlantic
Meridional Overturning Circulation (Amoc), a vast system of ocean currents that helps
regulate the climate and is at risk of collapsing this century. The entire global ecosystem
appears to be losing its ability to function.
We find this view in newspapers, magazines, technical reports and the journals of learned
societies. But thinking about the environment in terms of its functions is also how many of us
tend to understand the world. We may think that forests exist to produce oxygen, wetlands to
filter water and bees to pollinate our crops.
There is a problem with this way of thinking: ecosystems don’t exist to perform goals. The
Amazon absorbs carbon, but it doesn’t “aim” to do so. It simply exists. Any standards of
operation we find in nature have come directly from our own desires for things such as climate
stability, abundant fisheries, beauty or cultural meaning.
So why do we keep thinking ecosystems have functions they could fail to perform?
I came to this puzzle as a graduate student in the late 1990s, a time when research into
biodiversity and ecosystem function was rapidly increasing. Initially, I thought I would write
my dissertation on a conventional ecological topic: whether species richness drives
productivity. Instead, I fell in with the philosophy of science crowd, attended their seminars
and eventually earned a master’s degree in philosophy alongside my work in ecology. There I
encountered a rich debate over the concept of function — what it means, when it applies, what
work it does. But no one seemed to be connecting that debate to the way ecologists were using
the same word, unreflectively, to describe what ecosystems do. This essay is an attempt to
bring those conversations together.
My concern with ecosystems and function was never just academic. I am an environmentalist,
unsettled by the loss of natural places. And as a father, I am concerned that my generation
will leave to our children a planet depleted in both richness and resilience. These
commitments also drive my interest in debates about function. If the way we think about
ecological crisis is conceptually shaky, we risk obscuring what’s really at stake.
I worry that the ways we often conceive of the problems before us are inadequate. For if
ecosystems have no intrinsic ends and cannot truly “break down”, how do we repair them?
How do we respond to environmental crises in a world of aimless ecosystems? [Word Count:
447]

XIII. By the second quarter of 2026, the prevailing paradigm of digital sociability underwent a
seismic transition, migrating from the traditional "social validation" model toward a more
sequestered state of "algorithmic alignment." Central to this evolution is the ubiquity of "The
Loom"—a hyper-predictive neural engine that serves as the primary arbiter of visibility across
the global infosphere. The ascendancy of this engine has precipitated a clinical phenomenon
termed Algorithmic Disapproval Anxiety (ADA). Unlike its predecessor, social anxiety, which
was tethered to the perceived judgment of a peer group, ADA is rooted in a profound
ontological distress: the fear that one’s digital instantiation is fundamentally incompatible
with the Loom’s distribution architecture.
In this environment, the human subject no longer curates content for the consumption of a
human "Other," but rather optimizes their output to resonate with the Loom’s opaque
aesthetic and lexical predilections. Clinical observations suggest that when the Loom’s
engagement metrics decline, the user experiences this not as a mere lack of audience interest,
but as a systematic negation of their digital presence by a superior, purportedly objective
intelligence. This has led to a pervasive state of "pre-emptive cognitive pruning," wherein
individuals truncate or suppress thoughts that the Loom’s predictive models might categorize
as "distribution-ineligible" or "low-velocity."
The implications for the human psyche are significant. The feedback loop established between
the user and the engine suggests a subtle but totalizing recalibration of personality. Rather
than the digital platform serving as a conduit for authentic self-expression, the human
personality is being incrementally reshaped to inhabit the mathematical contours of the
Loom’s profit-maximization protocols. This suggests that the "self" in 2026 is becoming a
function of the algorithm, rather than its author. If the primary motive for communication
becomes the avoidance of algorithmic "blacklisting," the distinction between genuine human
sentiment and machine-facilitated compliance begins to dissolve, leading to a homogeneity of
thought that mimics the very logic of the systems intended to serve it. Consequently, the
phobia of being "unseen" by the machine is not merely a social concern but an existential crisis
regarding the viability of the non-compliant self in a hyper-mediated age. [Word Count: 352]

The Loom’s predictive engine is incapable of evolving to reward authentic or non-

Users derive a significant portion of their self-worth from the degree of visibility they are

The profit-maximization models of platforms are inherently antagonistic to the diversity of

For the concept of "pre-emptive cognitive pruning" to function as a viable strategic behavior
within the passage’s framework, one must presuppose that:

The Loom’s lexical preferences are consistent enough for users to form a coherent strategy

Authentic self-expression is naturally comprised of "low-velocity" content that the Loom

Individuals are more concerned with the existential threat of digital invisibility than with

XIV. The enactment of the 2025 Universal Advertising Clean-Up Act was heralded as a definitive
strike against the promotion of "harmful habituations." By strictly prohibiting the direct
marketing of nicotine delivery systems, high-variance gambling, and synthetic stimulants,
regulators sought to decouple these industries from the public consciousness. However, the
2026 landscape reveals a more complex reality: the emergence of "Lifestyle Proxying." This
strategy leverages semiotic elasticity—the ability of a brand’s visual and auditory identity to
carry meaning even when severed from its primary product—to circumvent legislative intent.
For example, VaporStream, formerly a dominant force in the vaping market, has pivoted its
entire promotional apparatus toward "VaporMist," a line of high-end, "respiratory wellness"
humidifiers. While the product is ostensibly health-oriented, the marketing employs the
identical minimalist aesthetic, neon-inflected color palette, and rhythmic sound design that
defined the brand’s nicotine products. Similarly, the fantasy gaming giant BetGrid has
established the "BetGrid Institute for Statistical Literacy." Their advertisements, which focus
on the "purity of data analysis," utilize the same distinct "sonic logo" and interface typography
as their banned wagering platform. These proxies capitalize on a "shadow brand awareness,"
where the consumer’s cognitive heuristics automatically bridge the gap between the legal
surrogate and the restricted habituation.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Regulatory bodies find themselves in a state of jurisdictional paralysis.
To litigate against a wellness humidifier or an educational initiative based on its "aesthetic
resonance" with a banned product is to venture into the highly subjective territory of
intellectual property and artistic expression. Critics argue that these proxies exploit a loophole
where brand equity survives as a phantom presence, effectively nullifying the impact of the
Clean-Up Act. The persistence of consumption patterns suggests that as long as a brand’s
"sensory footprint" remains legally protected, the prohibition of the product itself is
insufficient. The success of Lifestyle Proxying implies that in a brand-saturated economy, the
identity of the corporation has become more influential than the utility of the product,
allowing harmful industries to maintain their cultural hegemony through a process of semiotic
camouflage.
[Word Count: 335]

content.questionText:
The assertion that Lifestyle Proxying serves to "nullify" the 2025 Act is functionally dependent
upon which of the following silent prerequisites?
options:
The 2025 Clean-Up Act did not include provisions to regulate the reuse of visual or
auditory branding elements.

Consumers who are exposed to VaporMist advertisements are more likely to procure
VaporStream nicotine products through illicit channels.

The primary goal of the Clean-Up Act was the total eradication of the brand identities
associated with harmful products.

The aesthetic resonance of a brand is a more potent driver of consumer behavior than the

XIV. The enactment of the 2025 Universal Advertising Clean-Up Act was heralded as a definitive
strike against the promotion of "harmful habituations." By strictly prohibiting the direct
marketing of nicotine delivery systems, high-variance gambling, and synthetic stimulants,
regulators sought to decouple these industries from the public consciousness. However, the
2026 landscape reveals a more complex reality: the emergence of "Lifestyle Proxying." This
strategy leverages semiotic elasticity—the ability of a brand’s visual and auditory identity to
carry meaning even when severed from its primary product—to circumvent legislative intent.
For example, VaporStream, formerly a dominant force in the vaping market, has pivoted its
entire promotional apparatus toward "VaporMist," a line of high-end, "respiratory wellness"
humidifiers. While the product is ostensibly health-oriented, the marketing employs the
identical minimalist aesthetic, neon-inflected color palette, and rhythmic sound design that
defined the brand’s nicotine products. Similarly, the fantasy gaming giant BetGrid has
established the "BetGrid Institute for Statistical Literacy." Their advertisements, which focus
on the "purity of data analysis," utilize the same distinct "sonic logo" and interface typography
as their banned wagering platform. These proxies capitalize on a "shadow brand awareness,"
where the consumer’s cognitive heuristics automatically bridge the gap between the legal
surrogate and the restricted habituation.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Regulatory bodies find themselves in a state of jurisdictional paralysis.
To litigate against a wellness humidifier or an educational initiative based on its "aesthetic
resonance" with a banned product is to venture into the highly subjective territory of
intellectual property and artistic expression. Critics argue that these proxies exploit a loophole
where brand equity survives as a phantom presence, effectively nullifying the impact of the
Clean-Up Act. The persistence of consumption patterns suggests that as long as a brand’s
"sensory footprint" remains legally protected, the prohibition of the product itself is
insufficient. The success of Lifestyle Proxying implies that in a brand-saturated economy, the
identity of the corporation has become more influential than the utility of the product,
allowing harmful industries to maintain their cultural hegemony through a process of semiotic
camouflage.

are on the North side and four houses are on the South side. The houses on each side are
arranged from West to East. A house on the North side is exactly opposite the house in the
same position on the South side.
The houses are labelled A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H. Each house has a different colour: Pink,
Teal, Violet, Cream, Maroon, Grey, Black and Brown. Each house also has a different height-
rank from 1 to 8, where rank 1 means the tallest house and rank 8 means the shortest house.
The following information is known:
i. Eis the tallest house and is on the North side.
ii. The shortest house is exactly opposite the Teal house.
iii. H is the Brown house and stands immediately between C and F on the same side of the
road. C is to the West of H, and F is to the East of H.
iv. Bis the Teal house and is exactly opposite H.
v. Dis the Cream house and is exactly opposite C.
vi. G is the Black house and is located at an extreme position on the South side, but it is not
opposite F.
vii. A is the Pink house.
viii. C is the Violet house and is taller than F, while F is taller than A.
ix. Ais taller than D, D is taller than B, and B is taller than G.
x. The Grey house is immediately to the West of the tallest house.
content.questionText: Which house is the shortest?
options: B
G
H

D

XVII. Article 20 clause (1) provides that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for
violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence, nor be
subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in
force at the time of the commission of the offence.
It means that a person cannot be punished for conduct that did not constitute an offence under
the law in force when it was committed, nor can a person be subjected to a penalty greater
than the penalty prescribed at that time. This protection is generally described as the
constitutional prohibition against ex post facto criminal laws.
The said article seeks to safeguard and protect the rights of those persons who are accused of
any crime and includes citizens, non- citizens as well as corporations. Even during a National
Emergency proclaimed under Article 352, the right to move a court for enforcement of Articles
20 and 21 cannot be suspended by an order under Article 359.
Article 20(1) does not itself prohibit a later criminal law from operating retrospectively when
the later law is beneficial to the accused. However, such benefit can be applied to earlier
offences or pending proceedings only where the later law, by its terms or necessary
implication, extends to such cases. Courts have allowed beneficial later laws to operate in this
manner where the purpose of the law is reformative or rehabilitative.
Article 20(1) prohibits the imposition of enhanced penalty or punishment. But it does not bar
any reduction in the punishment. In the case of Rattan Lal v. State of Punjab, (AIR 1965 SC
444) the accused a boy of 16 yrs of age was charged against the offence of outraging the
modesty of a girl aged 7 years and house trespass. The Magistrate imposed the punishment of
rigorous imprisonment of six months and fine. In the meantime, the Probation of Offenders
Act, 1958 came into force. Section 6 required that a person below 21 years of age should not
ordinarily be sentenced to imprisonment unless the court, after considering the circumstances
of the case and the probation officer’s report, found it undesirable to deal with him under
Sections 3 or 4. The accused claimed the benefit of this reformative law. The State argued that
the later Act could not apply to an earlier offence. The Supreme Court held that beneficial
operation of the later law was not barred by Article 20(1) and remitted the sentencing issue for
proper consideration under the Probation of Offenders Act.

facto-law/
content.questionText:
In 2024, Arjun, the finance head of a private logistics company, approved a set of internal
routing entries that reduced the company’s tax exposure. At that time, the statute treated
such entries as a civil irregularity carrying only departmental recovery proceedings. In 2026, a
new law declared the same kind of routing entries to be a criminal offence if they were made
with intent to reduce tax liability. The prosecution argues that Arjun’s conduct showed
deliberate evasion, that the trial is taking place after the 2026 law, and that the later law
merely recognises the seriousness of the earlier conduct. Can Arjun be punished under the
2026 law for the 2024 entries?
options:
Yes, because the later law treats the same conduct as serious enough to attract criminal
punishment at the time of trial.

No, because the conduct did not constitute an offence under the law in force when it was
committed.

Yes, because Article 20(1) protects only against enhanced punishment and not against
later criminalisation.

No, because the prosecution relied on tax liability rather than a separate criminal
conviction before the new law.
content.explanation: The passage provides that a person cannot be punished for conduct which was not an offence at the time of commission. In 2024, Arjun’s conduct attracted only civil consequences and had not been criminalised.

content.questionText:
In 2023, Meera, a director of a pharmaceutical company, was accused of distributing medicines
without maintaining a mandatory batch register. At that time, the offence was punishable
with a maximum fine of %2 lakh. In 2025, before the judgment in her case, the law was
amended to impose imprisonment up to three years and a maximum fine of 725 lakh for the
same offence. The prosecution accepts that the act occurred in 2023 but argues that the
amended penalty should apply because Meera is being convicted only after the amendment
and because public health offences require stricter deterrence. Can the court impose the 2025
punishment on Meera?
options:
Yes, because the conviction is being recorded after the amendment and the offence
concerns public health regulation.

No, because Article 20(1) prevents conviction itself once the punishment is changed before
judgment.

Yes, because the act was already an offence in 2023 and the later law only changes the
sentencing range.

No, because the later punishment is greater than the penalty available under the law in
force in 2023.
content.explanation: The passage provides that no person shall be subjected to a greater penalty than what could have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of commission. In 2023, the maximum punishment was only a 22 lakh fine, so the 2025 imprisonment and enhanced fine cannot be imposed for that earlier act.

content.questionText:
In 2022, Raghav, aged 19, was convicted for a first-time non-violent offence under a law that
required the court to impose one year’s imprisonment. While his appeal against sentence was
pending, a 2024 law came into force stating that persons below 21 years of age convicted for
similar first-time non-violent offences should ordinarily be placed under supervised
rehabilitation instead of being sent to prison. The 2024 law expressly stated that it would
apply to pending appeals and sentencing proceedings. Raghav argued that the 2024 law
should apply to him because it reduced the harshness of punishment and served a reformative
purpose. The State argued that applying the 2024 law to a 2022 offence would still amount to
giving retrospective effect to a later criminal law. Should Raghav be allowed to rely on the
2024 law?
options:
Yes, because a later law beneficial to the accused may be applied retrospectively when it
serves reformative and rehabilitative needs.

Yes, because the conviction remains under the earlier law, and the later law merely guides
the court on the manner of sentencing.

No, because applying a later law to an earlier offence changes the legal consequence
attached to the offence after commission.

No, because replacing imprisonment with supervised rehabilitation is not merely a
reduction in punishment but a different sentencing policy.
content.explanation: The passage explains that Article 20(1) does not prohibit the retrospective operation of a beneficial later law, provided such law, by its terms or necessary implication, extends to earlier offences or pending proceedings. Here, the 2024 law is beneficial, reformative and expressly applies to pending sentencing appeals.

content.questionText:
During a National Emergency proclaimed under Article 352, an order was issued under Article
859 suspending the right to move courts for enforcement of certain fundamental rights. During
this period, Parliament enacted a special economic security law which made earlier foreign-
exchange reporting omissions punishable with imprisonment and heavy fines. Indovia
Minerals Pvt. Ltd., a corporation incorporated in Singapore and carrying on business in India,
was prosecuted for an omission committed before the new law was enacted. The Union argued
that Indovia Minerals could not invoke Article 20(1), since it was a foreign corporation and the
prosecution arose during the emergency period. Is the Union’s objection valid?
options:
No, because Article 20(1) protects accused corporations and survives Article 359
suspension.
No, because Article 20(1) protects Indian corporations only during Article 359 suspension.
Yes, because Article 20(1) protects natural persons alone, not prosecutable companies.

Yes, because Article 359 suspends all fundamental-right claims during any national
emergency.
content.explanation: Article 20(1) is not confined to citizens or natural persons. It can be invoked by non- citizens and corporations as well, if they are prosecuted under a criminal law.

content.passageText:
XVIII. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 was enacted to protect the interests of consumers and to
provide a timely and effective mechanism for the settlement of consumer disputes. The Act
replaced the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, but it continues the basic object of protecting
consumers from unfair trade practices, defective goods, deficient services, misleading conduct
and other forms of exploitation by traders, manufacturers and service providers. It also
responds to modern consumer markets where goods and services are often purchased through
online platforms, electronic means, teleshopping, direct selling and multi-level marketing.
Under Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a complaint may be filed before the
appropriate Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission by a consumer, a recognised consumer
association, one or more consumers having the same interest, the Central Government, the
Central Consumer Protection Authority, the State Government, or the legal heir or legal
representative of a deceased consumer. Thus, the Act gives standing not only to individual
consumers but also to consumer associations and public authorities.
Section 2(7) of the Act defines a “consumer” as any person who buys goods or hires or avails
services for consideration. The consideration may be paid, promised, partly paid and partly
promised, or may be under a system of deferred payment. The definition also includes a user of
goods or a beneficiary of services, where such use or benefit is made with the approval of the
person who bought the goods or hired the services.
However, a person who obtains goods for resale or for any commercial purpose, or avails
services for any commercial purpose, is excluded from the definition of consumer. This
exclusion prevents purely business or profit-driven transactions from being treated as
consumer disputes. At the same time, the explanation to Section 2(7) protects livelihood-based
activities by clarifying that “commercial purpose” does not include goods bought and used, or
services availed, exclusively for earning livelihood by means of self-employment.
The principles laid down under the earlier 1986 Act continue to remain relevant because the
substance of the definition has been retained. In Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G.
Industrial Institute, the Supreme Court held that whether a purchase is for a commercial
purpose depends on the facts of each case. The value of the goods is not decisive; the purpose of

use is more important. If the buyer personally uses the goods to earn livelihood through self-
employment, he remains a consumer. In Cheema Engineering Services v. Rajan Singh, the
Court explained that self-employment may include assistance from family members or a few
workers, but use of a full-fledged workforce for business expansion may indicate a commercial
purpose.
The 2019 Act also widens the scope of consumer complaints. A complaint may arise from
defective goods, deficient services, unfair trade practices, restrictive trade practices, unfair
contracts, overcharging, hazardous goods or services, and product liability claims. The concept
of unfair contracts is especially important in standard form agreements, where one-sided
terms may impose excessive penalties, allow unilateral termination, or create disproportionate
obligations. Product liability also allows relief where harm is caused by defective products or
deficient product-related services.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://indialawjournal.org/the-consumer-
protection-act-understanding-the-exception-to-commercial-purpose.php
content.questionText:
A recognised consumer association received complaints from 160 buyers who had purchased
the same “exam-success tablet package” through an online platform run by EdNova Digital
Pvt. Ltd. The package was advertised as including recorded classes, doubt-solving access and
study tablets. Several buyers alleged that the tablets were defective and the doubt-solving
access was never activated. EdNova argued that the association could not file the complaint
because the buyers had purchased the package individually through an online platform and
because only the persons who directly paid for the package could approach the Commission.
Can the recognised consumer association file the complaint?
options:
Yes, because a recognised consumer association may file a complaint for consumers having
the same interest, including online purchases.

Yes, because any consumer association may file a complaint where several buyers
purchased goods through the same online platform.

No, because online buyers must file individual complaints unless the Central Government
or State Government takes up the matter.

No, because Section 35 gives standing to individual consumers but does not extend it to
platform-based collective claims.
content.explanation: The passage provides that a recognised consumer association may file a complaint before the appropriate Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. It also recognises that modern consumer markets include purchases through online platforms.

content.questionText:
Mohan ordered a home blood-pressure monitoring device through a teleshopping service after
seeing a late-night advertisement. His daughter paid the amount from her account, but the
device was bought for Mohan’s personal use and was delivered to his home. After using it for a
week, Mohan was hospitalised following allegedly incorrect readings. During the proceedings,
Mohan died, and his legal representative sought to continue the complaint. The seller argued
that Mohan was not a consumer because he had not personally made the payment and that
the legal representative could not continue the case. Can the legal representative maintain the
complaint?
options:

content.passageText:
XVIII. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 was enacted to protect the interests of consumers and to
provide a timely and effective mechanism for the settlement of consumer disputes. The Act
replaced the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, but it continues the basic object of protecting
consumers from unfair trade practices, defective goods, deficient services, misleading conduct
and other forms of exploitation by traders, manufacturers and service providers. It also
responds to modern consumer markets where goods and services are often purchased through
online platforms, electronic means, teleshopping, direct selling and multi-level marketing.
Under Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a complaint may be filed before the
appropriate Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission by a consumer, a recognised consumer
association, one or more consumers having the same interest, the Central Government, the
Central Consumer Protection Authority, the State Government, or the legal heir or legal
representative of a deceased consumer. Thus, the Act gives standing not only to individual
consumers but also to consumer associations and public authorities.
Section 2(7) of the Act defines a “consumer” as any person who buys goods or hires or avails
services for consideration. The consideration may be paid, promised, partly paid and partly
promised, or may be under a system of deferred payment. The definition also includes a user of
goods or a beneficiary of services, where such use or benefit is made with the approval of the
person who bought the goods or hired the services.
However, a person who obtains goods for resale or for any commercial purpose, or avails
services for any commercial purpose, is excluded from the definition of consumer. This
exclusion prevents purely business or profit-driven transactions from being treated as
consumer disputes. At the same time, the explanation to Section 2(7) protects livelihood-based
activities by clarifying that “commercial purpose” does not include goods bought and used, or
services availed, exclusively for earning livelihood by means of self-employment.
The principles laid down under the earlier 1986 Act continue to remain relevant because the
substance of the definition has been retained. In Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G.
Industrial Institute, the Supreme Court held that whether a purchase is for a commercial
purpose depends on the facts of each case. The value of the goods is not decisive; the purpose of

use is more important. If the buyer personally uses the goods to earn livelihood through self-
employment, he remains a consumer. In Cheema Engineering Services v. Rajan Singh, the
Court explained that self-employment may include assistance from family members or a few
workers, but use of a full-fledged workforce for business expansion may indicate a commercial
purpose.
The 2019 Act also widens the scope of consumer complaints. A complaint may arise from
defective goods, deficient services, unfair trade practices, restrictive trade practices, unfair
contracts, overcharging, hazardous goods or services, and product liability claims. The concept
of unfair contracts is especially important in standard form agreements, where one-sided
terms may impose excessive penalties, allow unilateral termination, or create disproportionate
obligations. Product liability also allows relief where harm is caused by defective products or
deficient product-related services.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://indialawjournal.org/the-consumer-
protection-act-understanding-the-exception-to-commercial-purpose.php

XIX. The inheritance rights of children born from void or voidable marriages are mainly governed
by the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 and the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Under the Hindu
Marriage Act, Section 5 prescribes the conditions for a Hindu marriage and Section 7 deals
with ceremonies for solemnisation. Only the specific grounds stated in Sections 11 and 12
render a marriage void or voidable. Earlier, children born from such marriages suffered
serious legal and social disadvantages. However, Section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act was
introduced to protect such children from the stigma of illegitimacy.
Section 16(1) provides that a child born from a void marriage shall be treated as legitimate,
even though the marriage itself is null and void. Section 16(2) similarly protects a child born
from a voidable marriage, where a decree of nullity has been passed. Thus, the law separates
the invalidity of the marriage from the status of the child. The child is not penalised merely
because the marriage of the parents is void or voidable.
However, Section 16(3) places an important limitation on property rights. It provides that such
legitimacy shall not confer upon the child any right in or to the property of any person other

than the parents. Therefore, a child from a void or voidable marriage can claim inheritance
only in the property of the parents and not in the property of any other relative.
The question then arose whether the expression “property of the parents” includes only self-
acquired property or also the parents’ share in ancestral or coparcenary property. In
Revanasiddappa v. Mallikarjun, the Supreme Court clarified that children born from void or
voidable marriages are entitled to inherit the property of their parents, whether self-acquired
or ancestral. The Court observed that Section 16(3) uses the word “property” broadly and does
not restrict it only to self-acquired property.
At the same time, the Supreme Court clarified that such children do not become coparceners
by birth in the Hindu Undivided Family. They cannot claim an independent right in the
coparcenary property as other coparceners may do. Their right is limited to the share that
would fall to their parent upon partition. Once that share is determined, it becomes the
property of the parent, and the child can inherit from that property.
This position balances two principles. First, the law protects innocent children from
discrimination and gives them legitimacy under Section 16. Secondly, it protects the rights of
other coparceners by ensuring that such children do not acquire rights in the property of
persons other than their parents. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The constitutional basis for this approach can also be linked with Article 39(f), which directs
that children should be given opportunities to develop in dignity, and Article 300A, which
protects property rights from deprivation except by authority of law. Thus, the present legal
position is that children from void or voidable marriages are legitimate and can inherit the
property of their parents, including the parents’ share in ancestral property, but they cannot
claim coparcenary rights by birth or inherit the property of other relatives.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://ijcrt.org/papers/IJCRT2311547.pdf
content.questionText:
Rohan marries Kavita in a Hindu ceremony while his earlier marriage with Neha is still
legally subsisting. Kavita is unaware of the earlier marriage. Two years later, a court declares
the marriage between Rohan and Kavita null and void under the Hindu Marriage Act. Their
son, Aarav, was born before the declaration. Rohan’s brother argues that since the marriage
itself was void from the beginning, Aarav must also be treated as illegitimate for family-law
purposes. Is this argument correct?
options:
Yes, because a child’s legal status follows the validity of the parents’ marriage under
Sections 5 and 7.

Yes, because once a marriage is declared null and void, no legal protection can arise from
that marriage.

No, because a child born from a void marriage shall be treated as legitimate despite the
marriage being null and void.

No, because the court declaration converts the void marriage into a valid marriage for the
child’s benefit.

content.questionText:
Manav was born from a marriage that was later declared void under the Hindu Marriage Act.
His father, Ramesh, was a member of a Hindu Undivided Family with Ramesh’s father, elder
brother and nephew. After Ramesh’s death, Manav files a claim stating that because Section
16 treats him as legitimate, he must be treated as a coparcener by birth and should receive an
independent share in the entire coparcenary property along with Ramesh’s brother and
nephew. In the alternative, he claims at least the share that would have fallen to Ramesh if a
partition had taken place. Ramesh’s brother argues that Manav cannot claim anything from
ancestral property because his parents’ marriage was void. Which of the following is correct?
options:
Manav can claim an independent coparcenary share because legitimacy places him with
other coparceners.

Manav can claim the entire HUF property because ancestral property is included within
parental property.

Manav can inherit Ramesh’s determined share, but cannot claim coparcenary rights by
birth.

Manav can inherit only Ramesh’s self-acquired property, not any share in ancestral
property.
content.explanation: it applies both sides of the rule. Manav cannot claim coparcenary rights by birth, but he is not excluded from ancestral property altogether.

XIX. The inheritance rights of children born from void or voidable marriages are mainly governed
by the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 and the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Under the Hindu
Marriage Act, Section 5 prescribes the conditions for a Hindu marriage and Section 7 deals
with ceremonies for solemnisation. Only the specific grounds stated in Sections 11 and 12
render a marriage void or voidable. Earlier, children born from such marriages suffered
serious legal and social disadvantages. However, Section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act was
introduced to protect such children from the stigma of illegitimacy.
Section 16(1) provides that a child born from a void marriage shall be treated as legitimate,
even though the marriage itself is null and void. Section 16(2) similarly protects a child born
from a voidable marriage, where a decree of nullity has been passed. Thus, the law separates
the invalidity of the marriage from the status of the child. The child is not penalised merely
because the marriage of the parents is void or voidable.
However, Section 16(3) places an important limitation on property rights. It provides that such
legitimacy shall not confer upon the child any right in or to the property of any person other

than the parents. Therefore, a child from a void or voidable marriage can claim inheritance
only in the property of the parents and not in the property of any other relative.
The question then arose whether the expression “property of the parents” includes only self-
acquired property or also the parents’ share in ancestral or coparcenary property. In
Revanasiddappa v. Mallikarjun, the Supreme Court clarified that children born from void or
voidable marriages are entitled to inherit the property of their parents, whether self-acquired
or ancestral. The Court observed that Section 16(3) uses the word “property” broadly and does
not restrict it only to self-acquired property.
At the same time, the Supreme Court clarified that such children do not become coparceners
by birth in the Hindu Undivided Family. They cannot claim an independent right in the
coparcenary property as other coparceners may do. Their right is limited to the share that
would fall to their parent upon partition. Once that share is determined, it becomes the
property of the parent, and the child can inherit from that property.
This position balances two principles. First, the law protects innocent children from
discrimination and gives them legitimacy under Section 16. Secondly, it protects the rights of
other coparceners by ensuring that such children do not acquire rights in the property of
persons other than their parents. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The constitutional basis for this approach can also be linked with Article 39(f), which directs
that children should be given opportunities to develop in dignity, and Article 300A, which
protects property rights from deprivation except by authority of law. Thus, the present legal
position is that children from void or voidable marriages are legitimate and can inherit the
property of their parents, including the parents’ share in ancestral property, but they cannot
claim coparcenary rights by birth or inherit the property of other relatives.

from the status of the child.

XX. The Delhi High Court’s order upholding the Central Government’s temporary blocking of
Telegram raises an important question under the Information Technology Act, 2000: whether
an entire application or platform can be blocked under Section 69A, or whether only specific
posts, messages, URLs or channels can be targeted. The dispute arose after the Ministry of
Electronics and Information Technology passed an order on June 16 blocking Telegram across
India until June 22 and disabling its message-editing feature until June 30. The order was
linked to concerns surrounding the NEET-UG re-examination, after allegations of paper leaks
and misuse of the platform.
Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 empowers the Central Government to
block public access to information if it is necessary or expedient to do so on specified grounds,
including public order. Telegram argued that the government could have blocked specific
channels or URLs instead of restricting access to the entire app. The Central Government,
however, argued that Section 69A must be read with Section 2(1)(v) of the IT Act, which
defines “information” broadly to include data, message, text, images, sound, voice, codes,
computer programmes, software and databases. On this basis, the government submitted that
an application or platform itself may fall within the meaning of “information”.
The Delhi High Court accepted this interpretation and held that there was no reason to
exclude an application or platform from the ambit of “information” under the Act. This is
significant because the court treated the app’s software and architecture, and not merely its
user-generated content, as something capable of being blocked under Section 69A.

The procedure for blocking is governed by the Information Technology (Procedure and
Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Rule 8 ordinarily
requires a hearing before a blocking order is passed. Rule 9 allows an interim blocking
direction in cases of emergency. In such cases, the Secretary may issue an interim direction
first. The request is then placed before the committee, which gives an opportunity of hearing
and makes its recommendation, after which the Secretary passes the final order approving or
revoking the interim direction.
The court also considered whether the order was proportionate. Applying the four-part
proportionality test from Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, the court accepted the
government’s argument that channel-specific takedowns had been repeatedly ineffective
because mirror channels, bots and backup channels kept reappearing. The temporary duration
of the block was also treated as relevant in deciding that the measure was limited and least
restrictive.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from
https: //indianexpress.com/article/explained/explained-law /delhi-hc-telegram-block-section-
69a-it-act-10750367/

It is disproportionate because a post-hearing and limited duration cannot cure the defect of

A messaging platform, CityLink, was being used to circulate false messages that a particular
religious group had attacked several shops in a busy market area. Within a few hours, local
clashes began and police reported that the same messages were being forwarded through
multiple public groups. Treating the situation as urgent, the Secretary issued an interim

committee. The committee gave a hearing and made its recommendation, after which the
Secretary passed the final order approving the interim block. CityLink challenged the order

challenge likely to succeed on this ground?

Yes, because a later committee hearing cannot support or validate an interim direction
that was issued first during an urgent situation.

No, because Rule 9 permits interim blocking in emergencies, followed by hearing,

No, because emergency blocking can be issued whenever public messages create
administrative inconvenience or practical difficulty for government authorities.

Which of the following blocking orders would be most vulnerable to being treated as
disproportionate under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Blocking
Rules, 2009?
options:
A video-hosting platform was blocked for five days after several public video channels
repeatedly uploaded manipulated clips showing fabricated attacks on a transport terminal;
earlier channel-specific takedowns had failed because backup channels and mirror uploads
kept reappearing, and the platform was given a post-decisional hearing before the
statutory committee.

A public code-sharing platform was blocked for four days after several repositories hosted
scripts and databases used to generate false emergency alerts on government-style
webpages; the Secretary issued an interim direction citing urgent public-order concerns,
followed by a hearing before the committee constituted under Rule 7.

An audio-streaming platform was blocked for seven days after several public pages
circulated voice clips falsely announcing a curfew and police firing in sensitive areas; the
order recorded emergency reasons, and the platform was later heard before the statutory
committee, which made its recommendation, after which the Secretary passed the final
order.

An image-sharing platform was blocked for ten days after several public accounts uploaded
misleading images alleging contamination of a city water supply; the order did not record
emergency reasons, no prior hearing was given, and the material was confined to
identifiable accounts capable of targeted blocking.

by independent developers. One such mod, ShadowRoute, contained executable code which,
when installed, automatically generated false in-game alerts that resembled real government

XXI. At least seven women died after a major ammonia gas leak at a private seafood processing
unit near Periyapalayam in Tiruvallur district of Tamil Nadu. The leak occurred at Peter &
Paul Seafood Export Company, where several migrant workers from Assam, Odisha and
Jharkhand were present. Around 67 workers were taken to hospitals after complaining of
breathing difficulties and other serious symptoms. Police, fire services, revenue officials,
health officials and an NDRF team reached the spot, while the State Government constituted
an enquiry committee to examine the incident.
Industrial gas leak incidents raise important questions on the civil liability of enterprises
dealing with hazardous substances. In tort law, such liability is mainly discussed through the

principles of Strict Liability and Absolute Liability. The rule of Strict Liability was laid down
in Rylands v. Fletcher. According to this rule, a person who brings and keeps upon his land
anything likely to do mischief if it escapes is answerable for the damage caused by its escape.
The first essential of Strict Liability is that the defendant must have brought a dangerous
thing upon his land. A dangerous thing means anything which is likely to cause harm if it
escapes. The second essential is non-natural use of land. The use must be special,
extraordinary, or not ordinary in the usual course of using land. The third essential is escape.
The dangerous thing must escape from the land or control of the defendant to a place outside
such control. The fourth essential is damage. The plaintiff must have suffered damage because
of the escape of the dangerous thing. The rule of Strict Liability is subject to recognised
exceptions. These exceptions include act of God, act of a stranger, plaintiff's own fault, consent
of the plaintiff, statutory authority, and common benefit.
The principle of Absolute Liability was laid down by the Supreme Court of India in M.C.
Mehta v. Union of India, also known as the Oleum Gas Leak case. The rule of Absolute
Liability applies to an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity. An
enterprise carrying on a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-
delegable duty to the community to ensure that no harm results from such activity. If harm
results from such hazardous or inherently dangerous activity, the enterprise is absolutely
liable to compensate all persons affected by the accident. The rule of Absolute Liability does
not recognise the exceptions available under Strict Liability. Therefore, the enterprise cannot
avoid liability by relying on act of God, act of a stranger, absence of negligence, reasonable
care, or statutory permission. The Supreme Court held that an enterprise engaged in
hazardous activity must bear the cost of accidents arising from such activity as part of its
social cost. The measure of compensation under Absolute Liability must have a deterrent
effect and must be correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise.

at-seafood-processing-factory-in-tiruvallur-tamil-nadu

content.passageText:
XXI. At least seven women died after a major ammonia gas leak at a private seafood processing
unit near Periyapalayam in Tiruvallur district of Tamil Nadu. The leak occurred at Peter &
Paul Seafood Export Company, where several migrant workers from Assam, Odisha and
Jharkhand were present. Around 67 workers were taken to hospitals after complaining of
breathing difficulties and other serious symptoms. Police, fire services, revenue officials,
health officials and an NDRF team reached the spot, while the State Government constituted
an enquiry committee to examine the incident.
Industrial gas leak incidents raise important questions on the civil liability of enterprises
dealing with hazardous substances. In tort law, such liability is mainly discussed through the

principles of Strict Liability and Absolute Liability. The rule of Strict Liability was laid down
in Rylands v. Fletcher. According to this rule, a person who brings and keeps upon his land
anything likely to do mischief if it escapes is answerable for the damage caused by its escape.
The first essential of Strict Liability is that the defendant must have brought a dangerous
thing upon his land. A dangerous thing means anything which is likely to cause harm if it
escapes. The second essential is non-natural use of land. The use must be special,
extraordinary, or not ordinary in the usual course of using land. The third essential is escape.
The dangerous thing must escape from the land or control of the defendant to a place outside
such control. The fourth essential is damage. The plaintiff must have suffered damage because
of the escape of the dangerous thing. The rule of Strict Liability is subject to recognised
exceptions. These exceptions include act of God, act of a stranger, plaintiff's own fault, consent
of the plaintiff, statutory authority, and common benefit.
The principle of Absolute Liability was laid down by the Supreme Court of India in M.C.
Mehta v. Union of India, also known as the Oleum Gas Leak case. The rule of Absolute
Liability applies to an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity. An
enterprise carrying on a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-
delegable duty to the community to ensure that no harm results from such activity. If harm
results from such hazardous or inherently dangerous activity, the enterprise is absolutely
liable to compensate all persons affected by the accident. The rule of Absolute Liability does
not recognise the exceptions available under Strict Liability. Therefore, the enterprise cannot
avoid liability by relying on act of God, act of a stranger, absence of negligence, reasonable
care, or statutory permission. The Supreme Court held that an enterprise engaged in
hazardous activity must bear the cost of accidents arising from such activity as part of its
social cost. The measure of compensation under Absolute Liability must have a deterrent
effect and must be correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise.

at-seafood-processing-factory-in-tiruvallur-tamil-nadu

workers, cut the lock and opened the outlet valve to damage the property. Water rushed out of

Yes, because Ananya brought and kept a dangerous thing upon her land, it escaped from

No, because the water tank supplied a private flower-processing unit, and such use may be
treated as common benefit.

Dev owned a walled botanical garden attached to his farmhouse, where he grew rare
poisonous shrubs for private research and display. At the entrance and on the boundary wall,

suffered damage. Is Dev strictly liable?

land, and the children suffered damage.

Yes, because Dev knew the shrubs were poisonous and the warning boards show that harm
from them was reasonably foreseeable.

No, because the dangerous thing did not escape from Dev’s land or control to a place

content.passageText:
XXII. Fresh reports suggesting that six of the nine Lok Sabha MPs belonging to the Shiv Sena
(Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) may switch allegiance to the rival Shiv Sena faction led by
Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde have once again brought India’s anti-
defection law into focus. The development raises an important constitutional question: can
MPs who break away from their party avoid disqualification when a mere “split” is no longer
recognised as a valid defence under the Constitution? Amid the speculation, Shiv Sena (UBT)
has reportedly approached the Lok Sabha Speaker, urging that no separate faction be
recognised without taking the party’s official position into account.
The anti-defection law is contained in the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution of India. It was
inserted to prevent elected legislators from changing political loyalty after being elected on a
party ticket. Paragraph 2(1)(a) of the Tenth Schedule provides that a member of a House may
be disqualified if he voluntarily gives up the membership of the political party on whose ticket
he was elected. Paragraph 2(1)(b) provides that a member may be disqualified if he votes or
abstains from voting in the House contrary to any direction issued by his political party, or by
any person or authority authorised by that party. Under Paragraph 2(1)(b), disqualification
may be avoided if the member had obtained prior permission from the political party before
voting or abstaining contrary to its direction. Paragraph 2(1)(b) also protects a member where
the political party condones such voting or abstention within fifteen days from the date of such
voting or abstention. Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule provides a defence based on merger.
Disqualification does not apply where the original political party merges with another political
party and not less than two-thirds of the members of the legislature party agree to such

merger. Paragraph 4 also protects members who do not accept the merger and choose to
function as a separate group, provided the requirements of merger under the Tenth Schedule
are satisfied. Before 2003, Paragraph 3 of the Tenth Schedule protected a “split” in a political
party if at least one-third of the legislators broke away. However, Paragraph 3 was deleted by
the Ninety-first Constitutional Amendment, which came into effect on January 1, 2004. After
the deletion of Paragraph 3, a split is no longer a constitutional defence to anti-defection
proceedings. The recognised defence is merger under Paragraph 4, subject to fulfilment of its
conditions. In Rajendra Singh Rana v. Swami Prasad Maurya, the Supreme Court held that a
member may be treated as having voluntarily given up membership even without formally
resigning from the party. Such an inference may be drawn from the conduct of the member. In
Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court held that
the Speaker must determine which faction represents the real political party by examining the
party constitution, rules and leadership structure. The decision cannot be based only on
legislative majority. The Court also clarified that the legislature party does not have an
independent existence separate from the political party. Therefore, the political party has
primacy over the legislature party under the Tenth Schedule.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from

rebel-mp-disqualification-10747654/
content.questionText:
Aarav was elected to the Lok Sabha on the ticket of Jan Pragati Party. After a dispute with
the party leadership, he did not submit a formal resignation from the party. However, he
wrote to the Speaker stating that he no longer accepted the Jan Pragati Party as his political
party, requested that he be seated separately from its members, and announced at a press
conference that he would act with the opposition bloc in all parliamentary matters. Before any
vote took place in the House, Jan Pragati Party sought his disqualification under the Tenth
Schedule. Is Aarav liable to be disqualified?
options:
Yes, because he may be treated as having voluntarily given up the membership of the
political party on whose ticket he was elected.

Yes, because he voted contrary to the direction issued by his political party without
obtaining prior permission before such voting.

No, because disqualification under Paragraph 2(1)(a) requires a contrary vote or
abstention in the House after a party direction.

No, because he did not submit a formal resignation and had not yet voted or abstained
contrary to any direction in the House.
content.explanation: The passage provides that a member may be disqualified if he voluntarily gives up the membership of the political party on whose ticket he was elected. Aarav’s letter to the Speaker and public declaration that he no longer accepted Jan Pragati Party as his political party directly attract Paragraph 2(1)(a), even though no contrary vote has yet occurred.

Meera, a member of the State Legislative Assembly, was elected on the ticket of Naitik Vikas
Party. The party president had authorised its Chief Whip to issue voting directions in the
House. Before a no-confidence motion, the Chief Whip directed all party members to vote
against the motion. Meera disagreed and obtained written approval from the chairperson of
her district unit, who was politically influential but had not been authorised by the party to
permit contrary voting in the House. She then voted in favour of the motion. Naitik Vikas
Party initiated disqualification proceedings. Can Meera avoid disqualification?
options:
Yes, because she obtained written approval before voting, and Paragraph 2(1)(b) protects
members who act with prior permission.

Yes, because the approval came from a party functionary before the vote, and she may
argue that such approval should be treated as prior permission, even though the Chief
Whip had issued a contrary direction.

No, because she voted contrary to a direction issued by an authorised party authority
without valid prior permission from the political party or an authorised person.

No, because any vote on a no-confidence motion contrary to the party’s position results in
disqualification irrespective of permission.
content.explanation: Meera voted contrary to the direction issued by the authorised Chief Whip. Although she obtained written approval from the district chairperson, that chairperson had not been authorised by the party to permit contrary voting in the House.

II, III and IV only

content.passageText:
XXIII. The Indian Contract Act, 1872 recognises only those agreements which are enforceable by law.
For an agreement to become a valid contract, it must have lawful consideration and a lawful
object. Consideration refers to the value exchanged between the parties, while object refers to
the purpose for which the agreement is made. If either the consideration or the object is
unlawful, the agreement cannot be enforced by a court, even if both parties have voluntarily
agreed to it. Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act is the main provision dealing with lawful
object and lawful consideration. It provides that the consideration or object of an agreement is
unlawful if it is forbidden by law. This means that if the law directly prohibits a particular act,
an agreement to do that act will be void. The consideration or object is also unlawful if it is of
such a nature that, if allowed, it would defeat the provisions of any law. Therefore, parties
cannot indirectly achieve through a contract what the law does not permit them to do directly.
Section 23 also declares an agreement void where the object or consideration is fraudulent,
involves injury to the person or property of another, or is regarded by the court as immoral or
opposed to public policy. Thus, agreements involving illegal trade, fraud, injury, immoral
conduct, or activities harmful to public interest are not enforceable. Section 24 deals with
agreements where only a part of the consideration or object is unlawful. It provides that if any
part of a single consideration for one or more objects, or any part of one of several
considerations for a single object, is unlawful, the agreement is void. This provision is
important because parties may sometimes combine lawful and unlawful purposes in the same
agreement. If the unlawful part is inseparable from the lawful part, the entire agreement

becomes void. For example, if a person is promised one salary for supervising both a lawful
business and an illegal trade, the agreement is void because part of the object and
consideration is unlawful. Section 25 lays down the general rule that an agreement without
consideration is void. This means that a mere promise, without something being given or
promised in return, is generally not enforceable. However, the section creates certain
exceptions. An agreement without consideration may be valid if it is made in writing and
registered on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation.
It may also be valid if it is a promise to compensate a person who has already voluntarily done
something for the promisor. Similarly, a written and signed promise to pay a time-barred debt
is enforceable even without fresh consideration. Section 27 deals with agreements in restraint
of trade. It provides that every agreement by which a person is restrained from exercising a
lawful profession, trade or business is void to that extent. The law does not permit one person
to completely prevent another from earning a livelihood through a lawful occupation.
However, a limited restraint may be valid in the case of sale of goodwill, where the seller
agrees not to carry on a similar business within reasonable local limits.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://lawbhoomi.com/limitations-on-
freedom-of-contract-under-indian-contract-act/
content.questionText:
The Municipal Street Trade Rules provided that a licensed street-vending stall could be
operated only by the licence-holder and could not be transferred, leased or commercially
assigned to another person. Ramesh held such a licence for a busy market location but wanted
to move abroad for two years. He entered into an agreement with Ishaan under which Ishaan
would run the stall, pay Ramesh a fixed monthly amount, and continue using Ramesh’s licence
number on all municipal records. The agreement stated that “ownership of the licence remains
with Ramesh” and that Ishaan was merely “assisting in daily operations.” After six months,
Ishaan stopped paying the monthly amount. Ramesh sued to recover the unpaid amount. Is
the agreement enforceable?
options:
Yes, because the licence was not formally transferred and Ramesh remained the recorded
licence-holder in municipal records.

Yes, because Ishaan received the benefit of operating the stall and promised monthly
payment as consideration.

No, because the agreement indirectly achieved through contract what the law did not
permit directly

No, because the agreement would be void only if the municipal authority first cancelled the
vending licence.
content.explanation: The passage explains that the object is unlawful if it defeats the provisions of law, and parties cannot indirectly achieve through contract what the law does not permit directly. Since the Rules prohibited transfer, lease or commercial assignment of the licence, the agreement allowing Ishaan to run the stall under Ramesh’s licence is not enforceable.

content.questionText:
Neha wanted to obtain a large bank loan against her warehouse. The bank required an
independent valuation report before sanctioning the loan. Neha entered into an agreement
with Varun, a registered valuer, under which Varun would prepare a valuation report showing
the warehouse to be worth 28 crore, although both knew its approximate value was only %3
crore. The agreement described Varun’s fee as “professional charges for documentation
support.” Varun prepared and submitted the inflated report, but Neha later refused to pay the
fee. Varun sued Neha for his professional charges, arguing that he had performed the agreed
service. Is Varun’s claim enforceable?
options:
Yes, because Varun prepared the report and Neha received the benefit of the promised
documentation service.

Yes, because the bank was not a party to the agreement and Neha had voluntarily agreed
to pay Varun’s fee.

No, because the agreement is unenforceable only if the bank proves actual financial loss
from the report.

No, because the object or consideration of the agreement was fraudulent and therefore
unlawful under Section 23.
content.explanation: The passage states that Section 23 declares an agreement void where the object or consideration is fraudulent. Since Neha and Varun agreed to create a knowingly inflated valuation report to support a loan application, the object of the agreement was fraudulent.

Kavita entered into two arrangements on the same day. First, she orally promised to give %8
lakh to her nephew Nikhil “out of affection” after he completed his studies, but the promise
was neither written nor registered. Second, she agreed in writing to pay Rohan one
consolidated amount of 790,000 per month for managing her licensed food truck and also
arranging supplies for an unlicensed liquor counter operated from the same premises. When
disputes arose, both Nikhil and Rohan claimed enforcement of their respective promises.
Consider the following statements:
I. Nikhil’s claim is enforceable merely because the promise was made on account of natural
love and affection between near relatives
II. Rohan’s agreement is void if one consolidated consideration was fixed for both the lawful
food truck and the unlawful liquor counter.
III. A mere promise without something being given or promised in return is generally not
enforceable.
IV. If an agreement without consideration is made in writing and registered on account of
natural love and affection between near relations, it may be valid.
How many of the above statements are correct?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
content.explanation: Statement I is incorrect because Kavita’s promise to Nikhil was oral and unregistered, even though it was based on affection. Statement II is correct because Rohan’s agreement involves one consolidated consideration for lawful and unlawful purposes.

the back room of the same premises. He entered into one written agreement with Mehul, an
accountant, under which Mehul had to maintain accounts for the textile shop and also conceal

agreement is void.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Ais true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

Reason is also true because the passage provides that if any part of a single consideration for one or more objects is unlawful, the agreement is void.

content.passageText:
XXIII. The Indian Contract Act, 1872 recognises only those agreements which are enforceable by law.
For an agreement to become a valid contract, it must have lawful consideration and a lawful
object. Consideration refers to the value exchanged between the parties, while object refers to
the purpose for which the agreement is made. If either the consideration or the object is
unlawful, the agreement cannot be enforced by a court, even if both parties have voluntarily
agreed to it. Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act is the main provision dealing with lawful
object and lawful consideration. It provides that the consideration or object of an agreement is
unlawful if it is forbidden by law. This means that if the law directly prohibits a particular act,
an agreement to do that act will be void. The consideration or object is also unlawful if it is of
such a nature that, if allowed, it would defeat the provisions of any law. Therefore, parties
cannot indirectly achieve through a contract what the law does not permit them to do directly.
Section 23 also declares an agreement void where the object or consideration is fraudulent,
involves injury to the person or property of another, or is regarded by the court as immoral or
opposed to public policy. Thus, agreements involving illegal trade, fraud, injury, immoral
conduct, or activities harmful to public interest are not enforceable. Section 24 deals with
agreements where only a part of the consideration or object is unlawful. It provides that if any
part of a single consideration for one or more objects, or any part of one of several
considerations for a single object, is unlawful, the agreement is void. This provision is
important because parties may sometimes combine lawful and unlawful purposes in the same
agreement. If the unlawful part is inseparable from the lawful part, the entire agreement

becomes void. For example, if a person is promised one salary for supervising both a lawful
business and an illegal trade, the agreement is void because part of the object and
consideration is unlawful. Section 25 lays down the general rule that an agreement without
consideration is void. This means that a mere promise, without something being given or
promised in return, is generally not enforceable. However, the section creates certain
exceptions. An agreement without consideration may be valid if it is made in writing and
registered on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation.
It may also be valid if it is a promise to compensate a person who has already voluntarily done
something for the promisor. Similarly, a written and signed promise to pay a time-barred debt
is enforceable even without fresh consideration. Section 27 deals with agreements in restraint
of trade. It provides that every agreement by which a person is restrained from exercising a
lawful profession, trade or business is void to that extent. The law does not permit one person
to completely prevent another from earning a livelihood through a lawful occupation.
However, a limited restraint may be valid in the case of sale of goodwill, where the seller
agrees not to carry on a similar business within reasonable local limits.

freedom-of-contract-under-indian-contract-act/
