content.passageText:
XXIV. Extortion and robbery are offences against property, but they differ in their ingredients,
degree of force, and manner of commission. Extortion is dealt with under Section 308 of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Section 308 defines extortion as intentionally putting a
person in fear of injury to that person or to any other person, and thereby dishonestly inducing
the person so put in fear to deliver property, valuable security, or anything signed or sealed
which may be converted into valuable security. The essential ingredients of extortion are fear
of injury and delivery of property or valuable security.
The fear of injury may be directed against the victim himself or against any other person. The
threat must be real enough to disturb the mind of the victim and affect the voluntary nature of
his action. Mere threat of divine displeasure is not sufficient to constitute extortion. The fear
may relate to physical injury, injury to reputation, injury to character, or even fear of criminal
prosecution, whether the prosecution threatened is true or false. Where the fear relates to an
accusation of an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a
term which may extend to ten years, Section 308 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
provides aggravated punishment. Similarly, where a person is put in fear of death or grievous
hurt, the punishment may extend to ten years and fine. Delivery of property or valuable
security is also necessary for extortion. If a person merely obtains a thumb impression by force
and no property, valuable security, or signed, sealed or authenticated document capable of
being converted into valuable security is delivered, the offence of extortion is not complete.

However, if the victim is induced by fear to sign, seal, authenticate and deliver a blank paper
capable of being converted into valuable security, extortion may be complete. However,
delivery is not limited only to movable property. The terms “deliver” and “delivery” may apply
to both movable and immovable property. Therefore, compelling a person by force or fear to
give up a share in a house or landed property may also amount to extortion. Extortion is
different from theft and cheating. In theft, the property must be movable and is taken without
the consent of the victim. In extortion, the property or valuable security is delivered by the
victim, but such delivery is caused by fear of injury. In cheating, consent is obtained by
deception or fraud. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Under Section 309 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2028, in all robbery there is either theft or
extortion. Theft becomes robbery when, for the purpose of committing theft, while committing
theft, or while carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by theft, the
offender causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death,
instant hurt or instant wrongful restraint. Extortion becomes robbery when the offender is
present before the victim and puts the victim in fear of instant death, instant hurt or instant
wrongful restraint, thereby inducing delivery of the thing extorted. Robbery is punishable with
rigorous imprisonment which may extend to ten years and fine. If robbery is committed on a
highway between sunset and sunrise, imprisonment may extend to fourteen years. Under
Section 310 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, dacoity is committed when five or more
persons conjointly commit or attempt to commit robbery, or when the persons conjointly
committing or attempting robbery together with those present and aiding such commission or
attempt amount to five or more.

content.questionText:
Aman discovered that Bharat had once used a forged experience certificate while applying for
a private job. Aman met Bharat and said that he would send the documents to Bharat’s
employer and also file a criminal complaint unless Bharat transferred 73 lakh to Aman’s
brother within two hours. Bharat knew that the allegation was partly true, but he feared loss
of reputation and possible prosecution. He transferred the money to Aman’s brother. Aman
later argued that no extortion was committed because he did not threaten physical injury and
the money was not delivered directly to him. Has Aman committed extortion?
options:
Yes, because fear of injury may include injury to reputation or fear of criminal prosecution,
and Bharat delivered property due to that fear.

Yes, because any threat to file a complaint becomes extortion once the threatened person
decides to avoid public embarrassment.

No, because the allegation against Bharat was partly true and fear of prosecution can
amount to extortion only when the case is false.

No, because the money was transferred to Aman’s brother and not delivered directly to
Aman after the threat was made.
content.explanation: The passage explains that fear of injury may relate not only to physical injury but also to injury to reputation or fear of criminal prosecution, whether the prosecution threatened is true or false. Bharat transferred money because Aman intentionally put him in such fear.

content.questionText:
Ritika, a moneylender, suspected that Sohan was concealing assets to avoid repayment of a
debt. She took him to an empty shop, showed him a knife, and forced him to sign and place his
thumb impression on a blank sheet of paper. She then kept the sheet with herself and warned
him that if he did not repay the loan within a week, she would “turn the paper into something
useful.” No money, completed bond, or property deed was handed over at that moment. Sohan
later complained that Ritika had committed extortion. Is the offence of extortion complete?
options: No, because neither money nor any completed legal instrument was delivered to Ritika.

Yes, because a signed blank sheet delivered under fear may be converted into valuable
security.

No, because the threat related only to future repayment and not to immediate property
transfer.
Yes, because fear of physical injury alone is sufficient even without any delivery.
content.explanation: Ritika intentionally put Sohan in fear of physical injury and thereby compelled him to sign, thumb-impress and deliver a blank sheet to her. The offence does not require delivery of money or a completed bond in every case.

content.questionText: Identify which of the following situations is not robbery.
options:
Ravi quietly removed a gold chain from Meena’s bag in a crowded bus, but when Meena
caught his wrist while he was stepping out, he pushed her violently and ran away with the
chain.

Kabir entered Arjun’s shop, stood before him with a knife, and said that he would stab him
immediately unless Arjun handed over the cash kept in the drawer.

Neeraj called Sohan from another city and threatened to publish false allegations about
Sohan’s sister unless Sohan transferred %2 lakh to him by evening.

Farhan snatched a phone from Kunal’s hand and, while Kunal tried to block the exit,
Farhan twisted his arm to carry away the phone.
content.explanation: Neeraj’s act may amount to extortion because he put Sohan in fear of injury to reputation and induced delivery of money. However, it is not robbery because Neeraj was not present before Sohan and the fear was not of instant death, instant hurt or instant wrongful restraint.

content.questionText:
Prakash and Ritesh were co-owners of a small ancestral house. Ritesh threatened Prakash
that unless Prakash signed documents giving up his share in the house, Ritesh would publicly
circulate damaging allegations about Prakash’s daughter. Fearing injury to his family’s
reputation, Prakash signed and handed over the relinquishment documents. In another
incident, Sameer quietly removed Prakash’s mobile phone from his bag without his consent
and left the place without making any threat.
Consider the following statements:
I. Ritesh’s act cannot amount to extortion because delivery under extortion is limited to
movable property.
II. Ritesh’s act may amount to extortion because compelling a person by fear to give up a
share in a house may fall within delivery.
III. Sameer’s act may fall closer to theft because movable property was taken without the
consent of the victim.
IV. Sameer’s act may amount to extortion because Prakash lost property, even though
Prakash did not deliver it due to fear of injury.
How many of the above statements are incorrect?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
content.explanation: Statement I is incorrect because delivery under extortion is not limited to movable property. Statement II is correct because compelling a person by fear to give up a share in a house may amount to extortion.

evidence.explanation: Statement I is incorrect because delivery under extortion is not limited to movable property. Statement II is correct because compelling a person by fear to give up a share in a house may amount to extortion.

L	Nine years on, the pair’s new collaboration, The Book of Birds, aims to open all eyes to the
wonder and peril of 49 species on the British red or amber list of declining and endangered
birds. With paintings by Morris and words by Macfarlane, the book is a twist on the classic
field guides that inspired both authors, evoking the spirit and poetry of birds from avocet to
yellowhammer. Morris, who has sold more than 1m books worldwide, was galvanised by the
Reader’s Digest Book of British Birds as a child. “It opened my eyes to life that is not human
and is around me,” she said. “I hope there are young people who will find The Book of Birds
and that it gives them that anchor and also wings. I also hope it helps birds become visible to
those who don’t see them. It’s more important than any other book I’ve done.”
Macfarlane said: “We wondered what a field guide or bird book would look like if it asked not
‘what is that bird?’, but ‘who is that bird?’; if it worked to help readers not only identify birds,
but also identify with them. There are 3 billion fewer birds in North America than 50 years
ago; 600 million fewer in Europe. Our skies are thinner, our springs quieter. This is a savage
loss. We wanted, in paint and word, to pull birds back into focus and splendour — and warn
against their vanishing.” Morris, whose favourite painting in the book is of the shearwaters
she watches from her home on the Welsh coast, admits she is never satisfied with her bird
paintings. “Can you ever do justice to something so beautiful? The wildlife artist Charles
Tunnicliffe is so much more accurate than me, but I am always chasing a life-force and the
soul of a creature when I’m trying to paint.” The book, which took seven years to make, has
already inspired an exhibition at the Bodleian library, The Wonder of Birds, which opens on 6
May and features unseen work by the pioneering ornithological photographer Emma Turner,
art from the legendary 19th-century American bird illustrator John James Audubon, and
Percy Bysshe Shelley’s original handwritten annotations for To a Skylark. [Word Count: 371]

I.	When he was shown the manuscript of this paper, Israel Rosenfield pointed out that there are
other arithmetics, higher and simpler than the “conventional” arithmetic of operations, and
wonders whether the twins’ singular powers (and limitations) might not reflect their use of
such a “modular” arithmetic. In a note to me, he has speculated that modular algorithms, of
the sort described by Ian Stewart in Concepts of Modern Mathematics (Chapter 3), may
explain the twins’ calendrical abilities:
Their ability to determine the days of the week within an eighty-thousand-year period
suggests a rather simple algorithm. One divides the total number of days between “now” and
“then” by seven. If there is no remainder, then that date falls on the same day as “now”; if the
remainder is one, then that date is one day later; and so on. Notice that modular arithmetic is
cyclic: it consists of repetitive patterns. Perhaps the twins were visualizing these patterns,
either in the form of easily constructed charts, or some kind of “landscape” like the spiral of
integers shown on page 30 of Stewart’s book.
This leaves unanswered why the twins communicate in primes. But calendar arithmetic
requires the prime of seven. And if one is thinking of modular arithmetic in general, modular

division will produce neat cyclic patterns only if one uses prime numbers. Since the prime
number seven helps the twins to retrieve dates, and consequently the events of particular days
in their lives, other primes, they may have found, produce similar patterns to those that are so
important for their acts of recollection. (When they say about the match-sticks “111-37 three
times,” note they are taking the prime 37, and multiplying by three.) In fact, only the prime
patterns could be “visualized.” The different patterns produced by the different prime numbers
(for example, multiplication tables) may be the pieces of visual information that they are
communicating to each other when they repeat a given prime number. In short, modular
arithmetic may help them to retrieve their past, and consequently the patterns created in
using these calculations (which only occur with primes) may take on a particular significance
for the twins. [Word Count: 334]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from:
https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1985/02/28/the-twins-and-modular-arithmetic/

Il.	Veganism, like the Indian religion Jainism and other movements that preach a very purist
strain of non-violence to other beings, seems to me a response to this one side of our
contradictory perception of mortality — its catastrophic nature. Such movements take seriously
the catastrophe that is every single death of every single sentient creature, whether fly, rat,
frog or human. And so they say: not by my hands, not on my watch, not if I can help it. They
are anti-death movements, whose followers go to great lengths not to squash flies or
mosquitoes, let alone have big fat pigs killed on their behalf.
This horror at the death of other creatures is intimately bound up with horror at the prospect
of one’s own demise. Flies come and go in countless masses, mostly beyond my sight and care.
But when something happens that causes me to empathise, to become the fly, then its death
becomes terrible. Some clever research from the field of social psychology has demonstrated a
close association in our minds between animals, animal products, bodiliness generally and our
own mortality. The upshot is that these things give off a whiff of the Reaper that colours our
response to them. The studies are part of a body of work known as ‘terror management theory’,
which holds that our world views largely function to help us manage the terror of death. That
means all world views: in the case of religions such as Christianity with their promise of
eternal life, the link is very obvious, but secular belief systems have their death-defence-
mechanisms too, often closely paralleling the religious ones. For example, just as Christians
believe they will be resurrected by God, those who subscribe to cryonics — being frozen upon
death — believe they will be resurrected by scientists.
Veganism and, to a slightly lesser extent, vegetarianism both follow this pattern, as modern
secular parallels of Jainism. Their response to the terror of mortality is to attempt to create a
zone of non-death, a zone from which the Reaper has been entirely banished, visiting neither
flies, nor rats, nor us. In Jainism, the death-denial element is explicit: your ultimate reward
for keeping your hands unbloodied is to become godlike. [Word Count: 368]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://aeon.co/essays/if-death-comes-for-
everything-does-it-matter-what-we-hill

content.explanation: This option correctly captures the central idea. The passage interprets veganism, vegetarianism and Jainism not simply as dietary or moral systems, but as responses to the terror of death and attempts to create a symbolic zone free from killing.

Il.	Veganism, like the Indian religion Jainism and other movements that preach a very purist
strain of non-violence to other beings, seems to me a response to this one side of our
contradictory perception of mortality — its catastrophic nature. Such movements take seriously
the catastrophe that is every single death of every single sentient creature, whether fly, rat,
frog or human. And so they say: not by my hands, not on my watch, not if I can help it. They
are anti-death movements, whose followers go to great lengths not to squash flies or
mosquitoes, let alone have big fat pigs killed on their behalf.
This horror at the death of other creatures is intimately bound up with horror at the prospect
of one’s own demise. Flies come and go in countless masses, mostly beyond my sight and care.
But when something happens that causes me to empathise, to become the fly, then its death
becomes terrible. Some clever research from the field of social psychology has demonstrated a
close association in our minds between animals, animal products, bodiliness generally and our
own mortality. The upshot is that these things give off a whiff of the Reaper that colours our
response to them. The studies are part of a body of work known as ‘terror management theory’,
which holds that our world views largely function to help us manage the terror of death. That
means all world views: in the case of religions such as Christianity with their promise of
eternal life, the link is very obvious, but secular belief systems have their death-defence-
mechanisms too, often closely paralleling the religious ones. For example, just as Christians
believe they will be resurrected by God, those who subscribe to cryonics — being frozen upon
death — believe they will be resurrected by scientists.
Veganism and, to a slightly lesser extent, vegetarianism both follow this pattern, as modern
secular parallels of Jainism. Their response to the terror of mortality is to attempt to create a
zone of non-death, a zone from which the Reaper has been entirely banished, visiting neither
flies, nor rats, nor us. In Jainism, the death-denial element is explicit: your ultimate reward
for keeping your hands unbloodied is to become godlike. [Word Count: 368]

IV.	Mr. Foster was left in the Decanting Room. The D.H.C. and his students stepped into the
nearest lift and were carried up to the fifth floor. Infant Nurseries. Neo-Pavlovian
Conditioning Rooms, announced the notice board. The Director opened the door. They were in
a large bare room, very bright and sunny; for the whole of the southern wall was a single
window. Half a dozen nurses, trousered and jacketed in the regulation-white viscose-linen
uniform, their hair aseptically hidden under white caps, were engaged in setting out bowls of
roses in a long row across the floor. Big bowls, packed tight with blossoms. Thousands of
petals, ripe-blown and silkily smooth, like the cheeks of innumerable little cherubs, but of
cherubs, in that bright light, not exclusively pink and Aryan, but also luminously Chinese,
also Mexican, also apoplectic with too much blowing of celestial trumpets, also pale as death,
pale with the posthumous whiteness of marble.
The nurses stiffened to attention as the D.H.C. came in.
"Set out the books," he said curtly.
In silence the nurses obeyed his command. Between the rose bowls the books were duly set out
a row of nursery quartos opened invitingly each at some gaily coloured image of beast or fish
or bird. www.lawpreptutorial.com
"Now bring in the children."
They hurried out of the room and returned in a minute or two, each pushing a kind of tall
dumbwaiter laden, on all its four wire-netted shelves, with eight-month-old babies, all exactly
alike (a Bokanovsky Group, it was evident) and all (since their caste was Delta) dressed in
khaki.
"Put them down on the floor."
The infants were unloaded.
"Now turn them so that they can see the flowers and books."
Turned, the babies at once fell silent, then began to crawl towards those clusters of sleek
colours, those shapes so gay and brilliant on the white pages. As they approached, the sun
came out of a momentary eclipse behind a cloud. The roses flamed up as though with a sudden
passion from within; a new and profound significance seemed to suffuse the shining pages of
the books. From the ranks of crawling babies came little squeals of excitement, gurgles and
twitterings of pleasure.
The Director rubbed his hands. "Excellent!" he said. "It might almost have been done on
purpose." [Word Count: 382]
Source: Extracted from: Brave New World by Aldous Huxley

V.	The International Booker Prize is one of the world’s most prestigious literary awards
dedicated to translated fiction. It recognises outstanding books that are translated into
English and published in the United Kingdom or Ireland. The prize celebrates not only the
author of a work but also the translator, highlighting the important role translation plays in
connecting cultures and languages across the globe. Established in its current annual format
in 2016, the award has significantly increased international interest in world literature.
Unlike many literary prizes that focus only on English-language writing, the International
Booker Prize brings attention to stories, histories, and perspectives from diverse societies.
The___ prize money is equally divided between the author and translator, emphasising their
shared creative contribution. Over the years, the award has introduced readers to writers from
Asia, Europe, Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East, encouraging greater appreciation of
global literary traditions.
Winning or even being shortlisted for the prize often transforms a book’s international
reputation. Sales rise sharply, translations into additional languages increase, and authors
gain worldwide recognition. The prize has helped many lesser-known writers reach a much
broader audience beyond their native countries. The judging panel usually consists of writers,
critics, translators, and public intellectuals who evaluate books on literary quality, originality,
and the effectiveness of translation. The longlist and shortlist announcements generate
considerable excitement among readers and publishers each year.
In recent years, the International Booker Prize has become a symbol of cultural exchange and
literary diversity. By rewarding translated fiction, it promotes dialogue among nations and
reminds readers that powerful stories can transcend linguistic and geographical boundaries.
The award continues to strengthen the global literary community and encourages readers to
explore literature from different cultures and traditions.

VII. The Indus Valley Civilisation, also known as the Harappan Civilisation, was one of the world's
earliest and most advanced urban civilisations. It flourished between approximately 2600 BCE
and 1900 BCE in the northwestern regions of the Indian subcontinent, covering parts of
present-day India and Pakistan. The civilisation was named after the city of Harappa, where
its remains were first discovered in the 1920s.
The Indus Valley Civilisation is renowned for its well-planned cities, advanced drainage
systems, standardised weights and measures, and impressive craftsmanship. Major urban
centres included Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, and Lothal. The streets were laid out ina
grid pattern, and most houses had access to drainage facilities, reflecting remarkable urban
planning.
Agriculture formed the economic foundation of the civilisation, while trade connected it with
distant regions such as Mesopotamia. The Harappans produced pottery, beads, seals, and
metal objects of high quality. One of the enduring mysteries of the civilisation is its script,
which remains undeciphered.
Around 1900 BCE, the civilisation gradually declined, possibly due to environmental changes,
shifting river systems, and economic disruptions. Despite its decline, the Indus Valley
Civilisation remains a landmark in human history and a testament to early urban
development and cultural achievement.

grid pattern, and most houses had access to drainage facilities, reflecting remarkable urban
planning.
Agriculture formed the economic foundation of the civilisation, while trade connected it with
distant regions such as Mesopotamia. The Harappans produced pottery, beads, seals, and
metal objects of high quality. One of the enduring mysteries of the civilisation is its script,
which remains undeciphered.
Around 1900 BCE, the civilisation gradually declined, possibly due to environmental changes,
shifting river systems, and economic disruptions. Despite its decline, the Indus Valley
Civilisation remains a landmark in human history and a testament to early urban
development and cultural achievement.

The largest known Harappan inscription, consisting of a signboard with 10 symbols displayed

political decisions and military victories.

Harappa — It was a sacred religious text displayed near a temple complex for ritual and
ceremonial purposes.

Dholavira — It likely functioned as a civic, administrative, or commercial announcement
intended to be seen and understood by the public.

Lothal — It served as a port authority notice displaying customs duties and trade
regulations for foreign merchants.

grouping comprising four countries: India, the United States, Japan, and Australia. The
initiative was first proposed in 2006 and established in 2007 and was revived in 2017 amid
growing concerns about security, economic stability, and freedom of navigation in the Indo-
Pacific region.
The Quad aims to promote a free, open, inclusive, and rules-based Indo-Pacific.
Although it is not a formal military alliance, the four countries cooperate on a wide range of
issues, including maritime security, disaster relief, climate change, critical and emerging
technologies, cybersecurity, infrastructure development, supply-chain resilience, and public
health. Regular meetings of leaders, foreign ministers, and senior officials help strengthen
coordination among member countries.
One of the Quad's major areas of focus is ensuring peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific, a
region that has become increasingly important for global trade and strategic competition. The
grouping also supports humanitarian assistance and disaster-response efforts, reflecting its
broader commitment to regional cooperation.
For India, the Quad is an important platform for advancing strategic interests, enhancing
maritime cooperation, and deepening partnerships with key democratic nations. Over the
years, the Quad has emerged as a significant mechanism for addressing regional and global
challenges while promoting stability, prosperity, and sustainable development across the Indo-
Pacific region.

IX.	The Padma Awards are among the highest civilian honours conferred by the Government of
India. Instituted in 1954, these awards recognise exceptional achievements and distinguished
service in various fields, including art, literature, education, sports, medicine, science,
engineering, social work, public affairs, and civil service. The Padma Awards are announced
annually on the eve of Republic Day and are presented by the Government of India at a
ceremonial function held at Rashtrapati Bhavan.
The awards are divided into three categories: Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, and Padma
Shri. The Padma Vibhushan is awarded for exceptional and distinguished service of the
highest order, while the Padma Bhushan recognises distinguished service of a high order. The
Padma Shri, the fourth-highest civilian award in India, is given for distinguished service in
any field. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The selection process involves recommendations from the public and various institutions,
which are examined by a Padma Awards Committee. The committee's recommendations are
then submitted to the Prime Minister and the President for approval.
Over the years, the Padma Awards have honoured a wide range of individuals, including
scientists, artists, athletes, social reformers, and public servants. By recognising outstanding
contributions to society, the awards celebrate excellence, inspire public service, and highlight
the diverse achievements that contribute to India's cultural, social, and national development.

X.	The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) is India's primary legislation for dealing
with unlawful activities, terrorism, and threats to the sovereignty and integrity of the country.
Enacted in 1967, the Act was originally designed to prevent activities that threatened India's
unity and territorial integrity. Over the years, particularly through amendments in 2004,
2008, 2012, and 2019, it has evolved into the country's principal anti-terrorism law.
Under the UAPA, the government has the power to declare organisations as unlawful or
terrorist organizations and to take legal action against individuals involved in terrorist
activities. The 2019 amendment further expanded these powers by allowing the government to

designate individuals, and not just organisations, as terrorists. The Act also provides special
provisions for investigation, arrest, detention, and prosecution in terrorism-related cases.
Supporters of the UAPA argue that it is an essential tool for combating terrorism, insurgency,
and organised extremist activities that threaten national security. They contend that the law
enables security agencies to investigate complex terror networks and prevent attacks.
However, the Act has also been the subject of significant debate and criticism. Critics argue
that some provisions, particularly those related to arrest, detention, and bail, can potentially
affect civil liberties and may be vulnerable to misuse. As a result, the UAPA remains an
important yet controversial component of India's legal framework, reflecting the ongoing
challenge of balancing national security concerns with the protection of individual rights and
democratic freedoms.

options: United Activities Prevention Act
Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act
Uniform Anti-Terrorism Protection Act
Unlawful Actions Prohibition Act
content.explanation: UAPA stands for the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, which is India's primary law dealing with unlawful activities and terrorism.

The Supreme Court declared the sedition law under Section 124A IPC unconstitutional,

The Supreme Court ruled that the prohibition clause of the Criminal Law (Amendment)

associations; UAPA therefore introduced a Tribunal that must confirm within six months

content.passageText:
XII. Current: The Bombay High Court recently held that recording a conference call between two
officials of Maharashtra Metro Corporation Limited (MMCL) and sharing it with another
official would not amount to “spying” under the Official Secrets Act, 1923 (OSA), since the
MMCL office does not fall within the meaning of a “prohibited place” under the Act. An FIR
was lodged against Pravin Samarth, Assistant Manager of MMCL, alleging offences under
Section 3 of the OSA and Sections 43 and 66 of the IT Act. The allegation was that Samarth
recorded conference calls between senior officials and later shared them with another
employee. The prosecution claimed that this amounted to spying and unlawful disclosure of
departmental information. The High Court noted that the office of MMCL was not a
“prohibited place” and that the facts did not show any conduct prejudicial to the sovereignty,

integrity, or safety of the State. At the same time, it found that the unauthorised recording
and sharing of official communications could amount to dishonest and fraudulent interference
with computer resources and communication systems.
Section 3 of the OSA penalises acts of spying and other conduct prejudicial to the safety or
interests of the State. For the offence to be made out, the act must relate to information,
places, or communications covered by the statutory framework of the OSA, particularly where
the conduct concerns a “prohibited place” or implicates State security. Section 2(8) defines
“prohibited place” and ordinarily refers to strategic, defence, or security-sensitive locations.
The Court held that an MMCL office does not fall within this definition, and therefore Section
3 was not attracted merely because an official conversation was recorded and shared.
The Court, however, held that Sections 43 and 66 of the IT Act were attracted. Section 43
imposes civil liability where a person, without permission, accesses, downloads, copies, or
extracts data from a computer, computer system, or network, or interferes with its operation.
Section 66 makes such acts punishable where they are done dishonestly or fraudulently. The
Court observed that the unauthorised recording and sharing of conference calls fell within the
scope of Section 43, and the dishonest sharing of that information with another person brought
the case within Section 66 as well.
The Court also referred to the Maharashtra Metro Rail Corporation Limited Rules, under
which employees are prohibited from communicating official information to unauthorised
persons except in accordance with authorised orders or in good faith performance of duties. On
this basis, the Court held that the applicant’s conduct was not only unethical but also
suggestive of dishonest intention.

phone-calls-officials-sharing-spying-529973

XIII. Current: The Telangana High Court recently held that police officers do not have the power
to detain or seize vehicles merely because the driver is found in an intoxicated condition. The
Court emphasised that while drunk driving must be prevented, seizure of the vehicle is not an
automatic or lawful consequence in such cases. The petitioner had approached the High Court
seeking release of his vehicle, which had been seized by traffic police after it was allegedly
driven by a person in an intoxicated condition. The petitioner argued that such seizure was
contrary to the law already laid down by the High Court in earlier decisions. The State
contended that the driver had prior instances of drunk driving and that the petitioner had
knowingly allowed him to use the vehicle. The Court, relying on its earlier 2021 judgment,
held that although the intoxicated person cannot be allowed to drive, the police cannot seize
the vehicle solely on that ground and directed disposal of the petition in line with established
guidelines.

The Court clarified that while traffic laws prohibit driving under the influence of alcohol, they
do not confer unrestricted power upon police authorities to seize or detain vehicles merely
because the driver is intoxicated. The primary objective of the law is to prevent unsafe driving,
not to impose additional punitive measures beyond statutory limits.
The Court laid down that where a driver is found intoxicated, the police must prevent such
person from continuing to drive. If another person accompanying the driver is sober and
possesses a valid driving licence, the vehicle should be handed over to such person. Where no
such person is available, the vehicle may be temporarily kept in safe custody. However, the
police are under a duty to release the vehicle to the owner or an authorised person upon
production of necessary documents such as the registration certificate, identity proof, and a
valid driving licence.
The Court thus balanced enforcement of road safety with protection against arbitrary exercise
of police powers, holding that seizure must be justified by law and not based on mere suspicion
or convenience. It further clarified that prior instances of drunk driving or alleged negligence
by the owner do not, by themselves, confer additional powers of seizure unless specifically
authorised by statute.
Source: https://www.livelaw.in/high-court/telangana-high-court/telangana-high-court-
police-seize-vehicle-driver-intoxicated-529649

XIV. Nuisance: The term 'nuisance' is made up of the French word 'nuire' and Latin word 'nocere'
or 'nocumentum' which in legal sense means ‘annoyance' or 'harm'. The element of unlawful
‘annoyance’ is the only thing common to all nuisances. Nuisance has been defined under two
categories - Public Nuisance and Private Nuisance. Public nuisance is a crime whereas private
nuisance is a civil wrong. To constitute the tort of nuisance, the following essentials are
required to be proved:
1. Unreasonable interference: Interference may cause damage to the plaintiff's property or
may cause personal discomfort to the plaintiff in the enjoyment of property. Every
interference is not a nuisance. To constitute nuisance, the interference should be
unreasonable. Every person must put up with some noise, some vibrations, some smell,
etc. so that members of the society can enjoy their own rights. An unreasonable activity
cannot be excused on the ground that reasonable care had been taken to prevent it from
becoming a nuisance.www.lawpreptutorial.com
2. Interference with the use of enjoyment of land: It may cause either -
(1) Injury to the property itself: An unauthorized interference with the use of the property
of another person through some object, tangible or intangible, which causes damage to
the property, is actionable as nuisance.
(2) Injury to the comfort or health of occupants of certain property: Substantial
interference with the comfort and convenience in using the premises is actionable as a
nuisance. A mere trifling or fanciful inconvenience is not enough. The rule is De
minimis non curat lex, that means that the law does not take account of very trifling
matters. The standard of comfort varies from time to time and place to place.
Inconvenience and discomfort from the point of view of a particular plaintiff is not the
test of nuisance but the test is how an average man residing in the same area would
take it.

8. Damage: Unlike trespass, which is actionable per se, actual damage is required to be
proved in an action for nuisance. In the case of public nuisance, the plaintiff can bring an
action in tort only when he proves a special damage to him. In private nuisance, although
damage is one of the essentials, the law will often presume it.
Source: Law of Torts by R. K. Bangia
content.questionText:
Mr. A owns a small, aesthetic coffee shop in a quiet residential area. His neighbor, Ms. B, a
professional musician, begins practicing her drums for half an hour a day in a soundproofed
studio in her basement. Despite the soundproofing, the barely perceptible vibrations from the
drums are felt by Mr. A in his shop.. The vibrations are not loud enough to disturb his
customers, and no tangible damage has been done to the building itself. Mr. A claims this is a
nuisance. Decide on your understanding of the passage, the most legally sound option.
options:
Yes, because any interference with the enjoyment of one's property gives one a right to
claim the tort of nuisance.
Yes, because the interference is a result of a continuous unreasonable activity.
No, because the interference is minor and trifling nature.
No, because Ms. B has taken reasonable care by soundproofing her studio.

XV. Article 22 of Constitution: Article 22 is a fundamental right of protection against arrest and
detention in certain cases. Clauses (1) and (2) of Article 22 confer four rights upon a person
who has been arrested. Firstly, he shall not be detained in custody without being informed, as
soon as may be, of the grounds of his arrest. If information is delayed, there must be some
reasonable ground justified by the circumstances. The grounds of arrest must be informed in a
language understandable by the arrestee. Secondly, he shall have the right to consult and to
be represented by a lawyer of his own choice. This right too is not lost if he is released on bail.
Thirdly, every person who has been arrested has the right to be produced before the nearest
Magistrate within 24 hours of his arrest. In computing this period of 24 hours, the time spent
on the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the Magistrate is to be excluded. This
requirement is dispensed with if the person arrested is admitted to bail. Fourthly, he is not to
be detained in custody beyond the said period of 24 hours without the authority of the court.
Even if an accused is initially illegally detained, the detention becomes lawful when
subsequently he is arrested and produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours. But where
remand orders are obtained by the police from the Magistrate or a Judge without producing
the arrested person before such Magistrate or Judge within 24 hours, Article 22(2) is violated.
An undertrial prisoner need not be arrested separately for every criminal case pending against
him. A subsequent lawful detention is not vitiated by the earlier illegal detention.
The two requirements of clause (1) of Article 22 are meant to afford the earliest opportunity to
the arrested person to remove any mistake, misapprehension or misunderstanding in the
mind of the arresting authority and also to know exactly what the accusation against him is,
so that he can exercise the second right, namely, of consulting a legal practitioner of his choice
and to be defended by him.
Source: Constitution of India by V.N.Shukla
content.questionText:
An artist, commonly known by his stage name as Raffy in India, is arrested for painting
graffiti on a public building. At the time of his arrest, a senior police officer verbally informs
him of the charge but, seeing that the artist speaks only in a regional dialect not common in
the area, hands him a written document in Hindi, which Raffy cannot read. The police,
however, produces him before a Magistrate within 24 hours. Has the police fulfilled its
obligation under Article 22?
options:
Yes, because they verbally informed him of the grounds and also provided a written
document, thus fulfilling the requirement.

No, because the information was not provided in a language that the accused could
understand, thereby defeating the purpose of the right.

Yes, because the artist was produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours, which is the
primary requirement for a lawful arrest.

No, because the police should have given him a lawyer to explain the grounds of his arrest
at the time of arrest.
content.explanation: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: No, because the information was not provided in a language that the accused could understand, thereby defeating the purpose of the right. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

The detention is illegal because the police violated the 24-hour limit, even if only by one

The detention is lawful because the police produced him before the Magistrate and the one-

XV. Article 22 of Constitution: Article 22 is a fundamental right of protection against arrest and
detention in certain cases. Clauses (1) and (2) of Article 22 confer four rights upon a person
who has been arrested. Firstly, he shall not be detained in custody without being informed, as
soon as may be, of the grounds of his arrest. If information is delayed, there must be some
reasonable ground justified by the circumstances. The grounds of arrest must be informed in a
language understandable by the arrestee. Secondly, he shall have the right to consult and to
be represented by a lawyer of his own choice. This right too is not lost if he is released on bail.
Thirdly, every person who has been arrested has the right to be produced before the nearest
Magistrate within 24 hours of his arrest. In computing this period of 24 hours, the time spent
on the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the Magistrate is to be excluded. This
requirement is dispensed with if the person arrested is admitted to bail. Fourthly, he is not to
be detained in custody beyond the said period of 24 hours without the authority of the court.
Even if an accused is initially illegally detained, the detention becomes lawful when
subsequently he is arrested and produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours. But where
remand orders are obtained by the police from the Magistrate or a Judge without producing
the arrested person before such Magistrate or Judge within 24 hours, Article 22(2) is violated.
An undertrial prisoner need not be arrested separately for every criminal case pending against
him. A subsequent lawful detention is not vitiated by the earlier illegal detention.
The two requirements of clause (1) of Article 22 are meant to afford the earliest opportunity to
the arrested person to remove any mistake, misapprehension or misunderstanding in the
mind of the arresting authority and also to know exactly what the accusation against him is,
so that he can exercise the second right, namely, of consulting a legal practitioner of his choice
and to be defended by him.
Source: Constitution of India by V.N.Shukla

A famous actress, Ms. Sinha is arrested by the police at an airport at 1 PM on a Monday. She
is taken into custody, but the police, citing a flight delay, inform her that they will be taking a
later flight. They land at 4:40 PM later that day and travel to the police station from the
airport, where she is detained. The next day, at 4:00 PM, the police finally took her to the
Magistrate. Ms. Sinha’s lawyer contends that her fundamental rights have been violated.
Decide if there has been any violation of Article 22.
options:
The police have violated Article 22, as a flight delay is not a justifiable reason for not
producing her before a Magistrate on time.

The police have not violated Article 22, as the time spent traveling (via flight) is a
reasonable delay and should be excluded from the 24-hour calculation.

The police have violated Article 22, but the detention becomes lawful when he is produced
before the Magistrate on Tuesday.

The police have not violated Article 22, because the right to be produced before a
Magistrate within 24 hours is only applicable to arrests made within city limits.

XVI. Unlawful Assembly under the IPC: The Constitution of India guarantees the right to
assemble peacefully and without arms under Article 19(1)(b). However, this right is not
absolute and Article 19(8) of the Constitution allows the government to impose reasonable
restrictions on the right to assemble in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, or
public order. These restrictions can include limits on the number of people who can gather, the
time and place of assembly, and the use of weapons or other dangerous objects.
Unlawful Assembly means an assembly of five or more persons with the intent to commit an
illegal act or to execute a lawful act through unlawful means. Section 141 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 (IPC) deals with unlawful assembly. Whereas Section 189 of Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) deals with the same. The members of an unlawful assembly must have a
common object which falls under any of the following categories:
e To overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force, the Central or any State
Government or Parliament or the Legislature of any State, or any public servant in the
exercise of the lawful power of such public servant.
e To resist the execution of any law, or of any legal process.
e Tocommit any mischief or criminal trespass, or other offense.
e By means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to any person, to take or obtain
possession of any property, or to deprive any person of the enjoyment of a right of way, or
of the use of water or other incorporeal right of which he is in possession or enjoyment, or
to enforce any right or supposed right.
e By means of criminal force, or show of criminal force, to compel any person to do what he is
not legally bound to do, or to omit to do what he is legally entitled to do.
Source: hitps://blog.ipleaders.in/dispersal-of-unlawful-assemblies-under-crpc/,

office is located to protest. When company officials attempted to engage with the group, a
physical altercation broke out and the group collectively threatened the officials to concede.
What is the status of the group now?

This is an unlawful assembly, as the number of individuals in the group exceeds the legal
limit for a peaceful protest.
This is a protest under Article 19, as their intent was to only hold a peaceful protest.

This is an unlawful assembly, as the object of the group has changed with the use of
criminal force.
This is not an unlawful assembly, as the fight broke out due to the company official.

The members are not liable for unlawful assembly, because they were apprehended before

Only 4 of them are liable for unlawful assembly as they entered the property, thereby
committing an offence; the other 2 are liable for abetment.
All 6 of them are liable for unlawful assembly as they had a common object.

No, this was not an unlawful assembly, because the individual was not a member of the

SECTION IV
XVII. At Dubai’s Madinat Jumeirah, visitors moved quietly between installations, pausing to
photograph sculptural works, leaning in to decipher mirrored text, and standing longer than
usual inside sound-filled rooms that invited reflection. Beyond the fairgrounds, however, the
mood across the region was markedly different. In the weeks leading up to Art Dubai’s 20th
edition, headlines were dominated by the escalating conflict between Iran and Israel, travel
disruptions and renewed uncertainty across the Gulf. That contrast, between a region
confronting war and an art fair built around dialogue, memory and exchange, shaped much of
this year’s edition.
After weeks of uncertainty, including a calendar shift from its original April dates to May 15-
17 amid regional tensions, Art Dubai opened with a quieter energy. There was less emphasis
on spectacle, more space for conversation, and a sense that both audiences and organisers
were approaching the anniversary edition with different priorities. As Art Dubai marks its
20th year, the fair appears less interested in market theatre than in a more urgent question:
what role can culture play when the world outside feels increasingly unstable?
What began in 2007 as the Gulf Art Fair has, over two decades, evolved far beyond its
commercial origins. Today, Art Dubai stands as one of West Asia’s most influential cultural
institutions, mirroring both Dubai’s own transformation and the emergence of the region as a
serious force in the global art conversation. Its journey has been shaped by defining moments.
In its early years, the fair helped position the Gulf on the global cultural map, contributing to
a broader regional shift towards soft power, creative economies and post-oil cultural identity.
It has also navigated moments of controversy. In 2012, reports surrounding the removal of a
politically sensitive work by Iranian artist Khosrow Hassanzadeh sparked debate around
censorship, political expression and the boundaries artists negotiate in the region. The fair has
always been about more than commerce. In times of crisis, culture becomes something people
turn to for renewal, healing and connection.
Unlike many established art fairs that remain anchored to western markets, Art Dubai has
consistently positioned itself as a meeting point for artists, collectors and curators from
geographies often underrepresented in the global art market. Notably, while Indian galleries
were absent from this year’s edition, Indian artistic voices remained strongly present. Nearly a
dozen artists from India featured across the fair, underscoring the country’s enduring creative
influence on the region’s art landscape. [Word Count: 403]

dubai-20-cultural-powerhouse-dubai-art-fair /article70984890.ece

XVII. At Dubai’s Madinat Jumeirah, visitors moved quietly between installations, pausing to
photograph sculptural works, leaning in to decipher mirrored text, and standing longer than
usual inside sound-filled rooms that invited reflection. Beyond the fairgrounds, however, the
mood across the region was markedly different. In the weeks leading up to Art Dubai’s 20th
edition, headlines were dominated by the escalating conflict between Iran and Israel, travel
disruptions and renewed uncertainty across the Gulf. That contrast, between a region
confronting war and an art fair built around dialogue, memory and exchange, shaped much of
this year’s edition.
After weeks of uncertainty, including a calendar shift from its original April dates to May 15-
17 amid regional tensions, Art Dubai opened with a quieter energy. There was less emphasis
on spectacle, more space for conversation, and a sense that both audiences and organisers
were approaching the anniversary edition with different priorities. As Art Dubai marks its
20th year, the fair appears less interested in market theatre than in a more urgent question:
what role can culture play when the world outside feels increasingly unstable?
What began in 2007 as the Gulf Art Fair has, over two decades, evolved far beyond its
commercial origins. Today, Art Dubai stands as one of West Asia’s most influential cultural
institutions, mirroring both Dubai’s own transformation and the emergence of the region as a
serious force in the global art conversation. Its journey has been shaped by defining moments.
In its early years, the fair helped position the Gulf on the global cultural map, contributing to
a broader regional shift towards soft power, creative economies and post-oil cultural identity.
It has also navigated moments of controversy. In 2012, reports surrounding the removal of a
politically sensitive work by Iranian artist Khosrow Hassanzadeh sparked debate around
censorship, political expression and the boundaries artists negotiate in the region. The fair has
always been about more than commerce. In times of crisis, culture becomes something people
turn to for renewal, healing and connection.
Unlike many established art fairs that remain anchored to western markets, Art Dubai has
consistently positioned itself as a meeting point for artists, collectors and curators from
geographies often underrepresented in the global art market. Notably, while Indian galleries
were absent from this year’s edition, Indian artistic voices remained strongly present. Nearly a
dozen artists from India featured across the fair, underscoring the country’s enduring creative
influence on the region’s art landscape. [Word Count: 403]

dubai-20-cultural-powerhouse-dubai-art-fair /article70984890.ece

content.passageText:
XVII. What do mosquitoes and vampires have in common? Leaving aside their blood-sucking
tendencies, the pair share a strong aversion to garlic. Researchers tested insects’ response to a
selection of different fruit and vegetables, and discovered that the pungent allium may prevent
mosquitoes (and various other winged insects) from mating. By blocking the mating process,
the team hopes garlic can offer an eco-friendly and affordable form of pest control. The notion
of using garlic to deter blood-feeding creatures was proposed in 1897 by Bram Stoker in his
novel [Dracula].Maybe he was onto something.
The researchers did not set out to find birth control. Rather, the opposite. Shimaa Ebrahim, an
associate research scientist at Yale, wanted to find out if fruits or vegetables functioned as an
aphrodisiac for fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster). To do so, Ebrahim laid out a “fruit fly
buffet,” said Carlson. Purées from 43 types of fruits and vegetables were placed in individual
Petri dishes along with a female and male fly, who were monitored for an hour. While the
researchers couldn’t identify an aphrodisiac, they did notice something odd. In the petri dish
that contained the garlic purée, mating was “completely abolished”. The same effects were
observed when the experiment was re-run with other species of fruit fly — six out of seven
showed a sharp drop in mating behavior when exposed to garlic.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Additional observations revealed that the presence of the vegetable did not just prevent the
flies from mating. It stopped females from laying eggs. To find out if smell or taste was
responsible for the aversion, the researchers placed flies in one of two setups. In the first, flies
could smell the garlic but were unable to touch or taste the vegetable thanks to the addition of
a mesh barrier. In the second, flies could both smell and taste the garlic. The results suggest
taste is the key factor. Around 80 percent of flies mated when they were unable to taste the
garlic. In stark contrast, none of the flies mated when they could.
To dig a little deeper and find out what specific compound or compounds were responsible for
the insects’ repulsion, the researchers separated the chemical compounds within the garlic
purée. The answer was diallyl disulfide, a chemical compound responsible for garlic’s
distinctive odor. Fruit flies are not the only flying insect that has this receptor. Garlic also
appears to be repulsive to tsetse flies and Aedes vector mosquitoes — two insects responsible
for spreading disease to people and animals. This suggests the plant could be used as a
deterrent and a natural form of pest control that is inexpensive, safe, and easily accessible,
according to researchers.
[Word Count: 442]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://www.discovermagazine.com/garlic-
may-stop-mosquitoes-and-fruit-flies-from-mating-and-could-inspire-new-pest-controls-49116
content.questionText:
Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim that garlic could deter disease-
spreading insects through the same biological basis?
options:
Old folklore often connects garlic with creatures imagined as blood-feeding nocturnal
threats.

Aedes mosquitoes spread diseases, making inexpensive prevention attractive to public
health authorities.
Mosquitoes sense garlic yet mate normally after relocating to untreated nearby areas.

Garlic sprays remain cheaper than synthetic products in several mosquito-affected regions
worldwide.
content.explanation: This option weakens the reasoning because the passage relies on the idea that sensing garlic may help deter disease-spreading insects. If mosquitoes sense garlic but still continue mating after moving elsewhere, the receptor’s presence would not be enough for pest control.

content.passageText:
XVII. What do mosquitoes and vampires have in common? Leaving aside their blood-sucking
tendencies, the pair share a strong aversion to garlic. Researchers tested insects’ response to a
selection of different fruit and vegetables, and discovered that the pungent allium may prevent
mosquitoes (and various other winged insects) from mating. By blocking the mating process,
the team hopes garlic can offer an eco-friendly and affordable form of pest control. The notion
of using garlic to deter blood-feeding creatures was proposed in 1897 by Bram Stoker in his
novel [Dracula].Maybe he was onto something.
The researchers did not set out to find birth control. Rather, the opposite. Shimaa Ebrahim, an
associate research scientist at Yale, wanted to find out if fruits or vegetables functioned as an
aphrodisiac for fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster). To do so, Ebrahim laid out a “fruit fly
buffet,” said Carlson. Purées from 43 types of fruits and vegetables were placed in individual
Petri dishes along with a female and male fly, who were monitored for an hour. While the
researchers couldn’t identify an aphrodisiac, they did notice something odd. In the petri dish
that contained the garlic purée, mating was “completely abolished”. The same effects were
observed when the experiment was re-run with other species of fruit fly — six out of seven
showed a sharp drop in mating behavior when exposed to garlic.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Additional observations revealed that the presence of the vegetable did not just prevent the
flies from mating. It stopped females from laying eggs. To find out if smell or taste was
responsible for the aversion, the researchers placed flies in one of two setups. In the first, flies
could smell the garlic but were unable to touch or taste the vegetable thanks to the addition of
a mesh barrier. In the second, flies could both smell and taste the garlic. The results suggest
taste is the key factor. Around 80 percent of flies mated when they were unable to taste the
garlic. In stark contrast, none of the flies mated when they could.
To dig a little deeper and find out what specific compound or compounds were responsible for
the insects’ repulsion, the researchers separated the chemical compounds within the garlic
purée. The answer was diallyl disulfide, a chemical compound responsible for garlic’s
distinctive odor. Fruit flies are not the only flying insect that has this receptor. Garlic also
appears to be repulsive to tsetse flies and Aedes vector mosquitoes — two insects responsible
for spreading disease to people and animals. This suggests the plant could be used as a
deterrent and a natural form of pest control that is inexpensive, safe, and easily accessible,
according to researchers.
[Word Count: 442]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://www.discovermagazine.com/garlic-
may-stop-mosquitoes-and-fruit-flies-from-mating-and-could-inspire-new-pest-controls-49116
